The board exam guidances note that candidates "wrote the reactions or named the product instead of writing the observations," showing that students mix up observation with inference. The correction is to remember that a decomposition reaction must have exactly one reactant splitting into two or more products; simply producing a gas is not enough evidence on its own.

diagnosticQuestions.question: Define a combination reaction and give one balanced equation with the formula of each substance.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: A combination reaction, also called a synthesis reaction, is a reaction in which two or more reactants combine to form a single product. The key feature is that the number of products is fewer than the number of reactants. A well-known example is the reaction of quicklime with water. When calcium oxide (CaO) is added to water (H2O), it forms calcium hydroxide, Ca(OH)2. The balanced equation is CaO + H2O -> Ca(OH)2. On the left-hand side we have one calcium atom, two hydrogen atoms, and two oxygen atoms; on the right-hand side the same numbers are present in the single product, so the equation is balanced. This reaction is also exothermic because it releases a large amount of heat, which is why the mixture becomes hot enough to be used in whitewashing and in some heating applications. Another correct example is the burning of hydrogen: 2H2 + O2 -> 2H2O, where two elements combine to form one compound, water. In the exam, a full mark answer must name the type, write a balanced equation, and name the product.

diagnosticQuestions.question: Why is the thermal decomposition of calcium carbonate called an endothermic reaction? Explain with reference to bond breaking and bond making.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: The thermal decomposition of calcium carbonate is called an endothermic reaction because it continuously absorbs heat from the surroundings in order to proceed. When limestone, CaCO3, is heated strongly, the bonds inside the calcium carbonate are broken and new bonds are formed to produce calcium oxide (CaO) and carbon dioxide (CO2). The equation is CaCO3 -> CaO + CO2, with the heat supplied shown by Delta above the arrow. Breaking the strong bonds in the carbonate ion requires a large input of energy. Although some energy is released when the new bonds in CaO and CO2 form, the amount of energy needed to break the original bonds is greater than the amount released. Therefore the reaction has a net absorption of energy from the surroundings. As a result, the test tube or the surrounding air feels cooler, and the reaction stops if the source of heat is removed. This is in contrast to an exothermic reaction, where the energy released in forming new bonds is greater than the energy needed to break the old bonds. The ability to keep the heat going is what makes the reaction endothermic, not just the fact that it happens at a high temperature.

diagnosticQuestions.question: A student says, "All chemical reactions that need heat are decomposition reactions." Evaluate this statement.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: This statement is not correct, although it contains a small grain of truth. It is true that many decomposition reactions need heat to break the bonds inside a single compound, and that these reactions are endothermic. The thermal decomposition of calcium carbonate, the breaking down of mercuric oxide, and the decomposition of potassium chlorate all need heat. However, the requirement of heat is not enough to make a reaction a decomposition reaction. A decomposition reaction is defined by the number of reactants and products: one reactant breaks down into two or more products. The need for heat is a condition, not the definition. Many other types of reactions can also need heat to start. For example, the combination of hydrogen and oxygen to form water needs a spark or a flame to begin, yet it is a combination reaction, not a decomposition reaction. In cooking, many reactions need heat but are not simple decompositions. Therefore, the correct way to identify a reaction type is to look at the number of reactants and products and to write a balanced equation, rather than to rely only on whether heat is supplied. The heat tells us about the energy change, which helps us decide whether the reaction is exothermic or endothermic, but it does not by itself tell us whether the reaction is a combination, decomposition, displacement, or double displacement reaction.

diagnosticQuestions.question: In a laboratory, a teacher heats a white solid in a hard glass tube. A colourless gas is given off which turns limewater milky, and a white residue remains in the tube. Identify the likely reactant and the products, write a balanced equation, and classify the reaction type and its energy change.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: The observations strongly suggest that the white solid is calcium carbonate, commonly called limestone or marble chips. When calcium carbonate is heated strongly, it decomposes into calcium oxide (quicklime) and carbon dioxide gas. The colourless gas that turns limewater milky is carbon dioxide, CO2, which is the standard test for this gas. The white residue left in the tube is calcium oxide, CaO. The balanced equation is CaCO3 -> CaO + CO2, and the condition for the reaction is strong heating, shown by Delta above the arrow. Since the reaction requires a continuous supply of heat and absorbs energy from the surroundings, it is an endothermic reaction. Because a single compound, calcium carbonate, splits into two simpler substances, calcium oxide and carbon dioxide, the reaction is a decomposition reaction. A good answer in the exam would include all four parts: identification of the reactant and products, the balanced equation, the classification as a decomposition reaction, and the energy classification as endothermic. Missing any one of these parts would lose marks.

diagnosticQuestions.question: Design a simple classroom demonstration to show the difference between an exothermic combination reaction and an endothermic decomposition reaction. List the materials, the steps, the expected observations, and the safety precautions.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: The demonstration can be done with two small beakers or test tubes placed side by side on a heat-resistant mat. For the exothermic combination reaction, take a small quantity of calcium oxide, CaO, in a beaker and add a little water. Stir gently with a glass rod and place a thermometer in the mixture. The expected observation is that the mixture becomes hot, steam may be seen, and the temperature rises. The equation is CaO + H2O -> CaO(OH)2, and the conclusion is that a combination reaction can release heat to the surroundings. For the endothermic decomposition reaction, heat a small piece of limestone or marble chip strongly in a hard glass test tube using a Bunsen burner. Hold the test tube with a test-tube holder and direct the mouth away from students. After a few minutes, the solid crumbles and a colourless gas is evolved; when this gas is bubbled through limewater, the limewater turns milky. The residue left is calcium oxide. The equation is CaCO3 -> CaO + CO2, and the conclusion is that a decomposition reaction can absorb heat from the surroundings. Safety precautions include wearing safety goggles and a lab coat, tying back long hair, keeping the mouth of the heated test tube away from people, using tongs or a holder for the hot tube, and ensuring good ventilation because carbon dioxide is produced. The demonstration clearly contrasts the two reaction types: one gives out heat as substances combine, while the other takes in heat as a single substance splits apart.

masteryCriteria: Can define combination reactions (two or more substances combine: C + O2 -> CO2) and decomposition reactions (a substance breaks down: 2HgO -> 2Hg + O2); can give two examples of each with balanced equations; can classify five reactions as combination or decomposition.

title: Chemical reactions - displacement and double displacement
subject: chem
definition: A displacement reaction is a chemical reaction in which a more reactive element replaces a less reactive element from its compound. In the context of metals, the reactivity series arranges metals in order of their reactivity, with the most reactive metals at the top and the least reactive at the bottom. A metal higher in the reactivity series can displace a metal lower in the series from a solution of its salt. For example, zinc, being more reactive than copper, displaces copper from copper sulphate solution. The blue colour of the solution fades as zinc sulphate forms and reddish-brown copper metal gets deposited. The balanced equation for this reaction is Zn + CuSO4 -> ZnSO4 + Cu. A double displacement reaction, on the other hand, is one in which two compounds exchange their ions to form two new compounds. When sodium chloride solution is mixed with silver nitrate solution, the sodium ion and silver ion exchange partners. A white precipitate of silver chloride is formed, while sodium nitrate remains in solution. The balanced equation is NaCl + AgNO3 -> AgCl + NaNO3. To predict whether a displacement reaction will occur, a student must know the reactivity series. Metals such as magnesium, aluminium, zinc, iron, copper and silver can be arranged in decreasing order of reactivity as Mg > Al > Zn > Fe > Cu > Ag. This means magnesium can displace aluminium, zinc, iron, copper and silver from their salt solutions, while copper cannot displace zinc or iron but can displace silver. Understanding an ion as a charged particle that can move and swap places is essential, because displacement and double displacement both involve the movement of ions in solution. Writing a balanced equation ensures that the number of atoms of each element is the same on both sides of the equation, which is a skill expected of every Class 7 student tackling ICSE Chemistry.
eli5: Some metals are like strong players in a game. A strong metal can push a weaker metal out of its team. Zinc is stronger than copper, so it pushes copper out of copper sulphate and takes its place. In a double displacement, two teams swap one player each, like NaCl and AgNO3 exchanging ions to make AgCl and NaNO3. The reactivity series is just a list that tells you which metal is the strongest.

misconceptions.belief: Students often think that any metal placed in any salt solution will react. The board examiner observation from 2024 notes that many candidates were unable to provide balanced equations and often got the products incorrect. The correction is that a displacement reaction only happens if the metal added is higher in the reactivity series than the metal in the compound. If it is lower, there is no reaction. For example, copper cannot displace zinc from zinc sulphate.

Students confuse double displacement with displacement. They see a new substance forming and assume one element has replaced another. This is similar to the examiner observation that candidates were confused between addition, substitution and oxidation reactions. The correction is to look at the reactants: in a double displacement, both reactants are compounds, and both positive and negative ions swap partners. In a displacement, one reactant is an element and it replaces another element in a compound.

Students write the reactivity series from memory but forget that it is a tool for prediction. The exam guidanceed that some candidates knew facts but could not apply them. The correction is to use the reactivity series actively: compare the two metals, decide which is more reactive, and then state whether displacement will occur and what the products will be. Simply listing the series is not enough; the board wants you to predict.

diagnosticQuestions.question: Define a displacement reaction and give one example with a balanced equation.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: A displacement reaction is a chemical reaction in which a more reactive element takes the place of a less reactive element in a compound. In metal chemistry, a more reactive metal displaces a less reactive metal from an aqueous solution of its salt. The classic example given in the ICSE Class 7 syllabus is the reaction of zinc with copper sulphate. Zinc is placed above copper in the reactivity series, which means zinc is more reactive. When a strip of zinc is dipped into blue copper sulphate solution, zinc displaces copper from the compound. The blue colour of copper sulphate slowly disappears because the Cu2+ ions are being removed, and colourless zinc sulphate forms in the solution. At the same time, reddish-brown copper metal is deposited on the zinc strip. The balanced equation for this reaction is Zn + CuSO4 -> ZnSO4 + Cu. To check that the equation is balanced, count the atoms on each side. On the left there is one zinc atom, one copper atom, one sulphur atom and four oxygen atoms. On the right the same atoms appear in the same numbers, so the equation is balanced. This reaction is also a good example of a redox reaction in later classes, but at this stage it is enough to recognise it as displacement based on the reactivity series.

diagnosticQuestions.question: Explain why a copper strip dipped in zinc sulphate solution does not show any change, while a zinc strip dipped in copper sulphate solution turns the solution colourless and deposits a brown solid.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: The reason lies in the relative positions of copper and zinc in the reactivity series. The reactivity series arranges metals in order of decreasing reactivity, and the series relevant here is Mg > Al > Zn > Fe > Cu > Ag. Zinc is above copper, which means zinc is more reactive. A more reactive metal has a greater tendency to form ions and enter solution, so it can displace a less reactive metal from its salt. Therefore, when a zinc strip is placed in copper sulphate solution, zinc atoms lose electrons to become Zn2+ ions and enter the solution, while Cu2+ ions in copper sulphate gain electrons and become copper atoms, depositing as reddish-brown metal. The blue colour disappears because the Cu2+ ions are consumed and replaced by colourless Zn2+ ions. On the other hand, copper is below zinc in the reactivity series, so copper is less reactive. It does not have enough tendency to displace zinc from zinc sulphate. No ions are exchanged, no new substance is formed, and the solution remains colourless with the copper strip unchanged. This is why predicting displacement requires comparing the two metals using the reactivity series, not just memorising a list.

diagnosticQuestions.question: A student says, "Double displacement reactions always produce a precipitate, so they are easier to identify than displacement reactions." Evaluate this statement.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: The statement is only partly correct and needs careful evaluation. It is true that many double displacement reactions in the school laboratory are recognised by the formation of a precipitate. For example, when sodium chloride solution reacts with silver nitrate solution, a white precipitate of silver chloride forms: NaCl + AgNO3 -> AgCl + NaNO3. The insoluble solid is a clear sign that a new substance has been produced, and this makes the reaction easy to observe. In this sense, the first part of the statement is correct for common classroom examples. However, the statement is not completely true because a precipitate is not necessary for a double displacement reaction. A double displacement reaction is defined by the exchange of ions between two compounds, and the products may both remain dissolved in some cases. For example, sodium hydroxide reacting with hydrochloric acid is also a double displacement reaction, but the products are water and sodium chloride, which stays in solution; no precipitate is seen. Therefore, the claim that double displacement reactions "always" produce a precipitate is false. As for the second part of the statement, double displacement reactions are not always easier to identify than displacement reactions. Displacement reactions can also be easy to identify when the colour of the solution changes, for example the blue colour of copper sulphate fading to colourless, or when a metal is deposited on a strip. The difficulty of identification depends on what evidence is available, not on the type of reaction. So the student's statement overgeneralises the role of a precipitate and underestimates the observable changes in displacement reactions. A better conclusion would be that both reaction types can be identified by careful observation of colour changes, precipitate formation and metal deposition, and the reactivity series helps in predicting displacement while ion exchange helps in predicting double displacement.

diagnosticQuestions.question: You are given four metals: copper, iron, magnesium and silver. Use the reactivity series to predict which metal can displace which others from their salt solutions. Also write a balanced equation for one displacement that will occur and one that will not.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: The reactivity series from most reactive to least reactive is magnesium, aluminium, zinc, iron, copper and silver. From the four metals given, the order is Mg > Fe > Cu > Ag. Magnesium is the most reactive, so it can displace iron, copper and silver from their salt solutions. Iron is less reactive than magnesium but more reactive than copper and silver, so iron can displace copper and silver but not magnesium. Copper can displace silver because silver is below copper, but copper cannot displace magnesium or iron. Silver is the least reactive and cannot displace any of the other three metals. A balanced equation for a reaction that will occur is Fe + CuSO4 -> FeSO4 + Cu. Here iron is more reactive than copper, so it displaces copper from copper sulphate. The iron strip will become coated with reddish-brown copper, and the blue solution will turn pale green due to iron sulphate. A reaction that will not occur is Cu + MgSO4 -> no reaction. Because copper is below magnesium, it cannot displace magnesium. Writing "no reaction" as the result is itself a valid prediction based on the reactivity series. This kind of question is common in the ICSE paper, and the examiner expects the student to give both the prediction and the reason from the reactivity series.

diagnosticQuestions.question: Design a simple laboratory activity to show the difference between a displacement reaction and a double displacement reaction. List the chemicals, the expected observations and the safety precautions.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: The activity can be done in two parts using simple solutions available in a school laboratory. For the displacement reaction, take a clean strip of zinc metal and place it in a test tube containing freshly prepared blue copper sulphate solution. Keep the test tube undisturbed for some time. The expected observation is that the blue colour of the solution slowly fades and a reddish-brown coating of copper metal appears on the zinc strip. The reaction is Zn + CuSO4 -> ZnSO4 + Cu. For the double displacement reaction, take two test tubes. In one, place a small amount of sodium chloride solution, and in the other, place silver nitrate solution. Mix the two solutions. The expected observation is the immediate formation of a white, curdy precipitate of silver chloride, which can be tested by its insolubility in dilute nitric acid. The reaction is NaCl + AgNO3 -> AgCl + NaNO3. Safety precautions for both parts include wearing safety goggles and a lab coat, handling silver nitrate with care because it stains the skin and is corrosive, not touching chemicals with bare hands, and disposing of the waste as instructed by the teacher. The comparison between the two activities shows that in displacement a single element replaces another element, while in double displacement two compounds exchange ions and a precipitate is often the visible evidence. This activity also helps students remember that the reactivity series is the key to predicting the first reaction, while solubility rules and ion exchange are the key to predicting the second.

masteryCriteria: Can define displacement reactions (more reactive metal displaces less reactive: Fe + CuSO4 -> FeSO4 + Cu) and double displacement reactions (ions exchange: AgNO3 + NaCl -> AgCl + NaNO3); can give two examples of each with balanced equations; can identify the precipitate in a double displacement reaction.

title: Kinetic theory of matter
subject: chem
definition: The kinetic theory of matter is a powerful model that explains what matter is made of and how it behaves by imagining every substance as an enormous collection of tiny particles that are always moving. According to this theory, all matter is composed of very small particles called atoms or molecules. These particles are in a state of continuous, random motion, which means they never sit perfectly still. The speed and energy of this motion depend directly on temperature: the more heat energy a substance has, the faster its particles move. The theory rests on several main postulates. First, matter is made up of a very large number of tiny particles. Second, these particles are always moving, and their average kinetic energy is related to the temperature of the substance. Third, there are spaces between the particles, and these spaces are very small in solids, slightly larger in liquids, and very large in gases. Fourth, particles attract one another, and this attraction is strongest in solids, moderate in liquids, and almost negligible in gases. Fifth, particles collide with one another and with the walls of their container; these collisions help the substance change state when energy is added or removed. The change of state of matter, such as melting, boiling, freezing, or condensation, can therefore be understood in terms of inter particle space, inter particle attraction, and the energy of particle motion. When ice melts, for example, the heat energy makes the water particles vibrate more violently until the attraction between them can no longer hold them in fixed positions. They break away from their rigid lattice and move more freely as a liquid. When water boils, the particles gain enough energy to overcome the attractions completely and spread far apart as a gas. The law of conservation of mass adds another important idea: during any physical or chemical change, the total mass of all the reactants equals the total mass of all the products. This means that matter cannot be created or destroyed in ordinary changes. If barium chloride reacts with sodium sulphate to form barium sulphate and sodium chloride, the total mass before and after the reaction remains the same. Even though the particles rearrange themselves into new substances, the number and mass of the particles stay constant.
eli5: Everything around you is made of tiny moving bits called particles. In a solid, they are close together and only wiggle. In a liquid, they slide around. In a gas, they zoom far apart. When you heat something, the particles move faster and can change from one form to another. Also, when things react, the total stuff does not disappear; it just gets rearranged.

misconceptions.belief: Students often write only part of a scientific statement, believing the examiner will fill in the rest. This mirrors the board examiner observation from 2024 that many candidates wrote only "concentrated" and lost marks for not giving the full phrase "concentrated sulphuric acid." In this chapter, a common version of this error is writing "mass stays the same" instead of the full statement: "Mass is neither created nor destroyed in a chemical reaction, so the total mass of the reactants is equal to the total mass of the products.
misconceptions.correction: Always write the complete, formal statement of the law of conservation of mass and follow it with a labelled example such as BaCl2 + Na2SO4 giving BaSO4 + 2NaCl.

misconceptions.belief: Students frequently confuse two closely related ideas, just as the 2024 board examiners noted the confusion between "excess of chlorine with ammonia" and "excess of ammonia with chlorine." In the kinetic theory, students often mix up inter particle space and inter particle attraction. They may say that solids have less attraction when they mean less space, or that gases have more attraction when they mean more space.
misconceptions.correction: Learn them as separate ideas. Inter particle space is about the gap between particles. Inter particle attraction is about the force pulling particles together. In solids, space is small and attraction is strong. In gases, space is large and attraction is very weak. Test yourself by writing the two terms and filling the blank for each state.

misconceptions.belief: Students sometimes believe that a substance changes its identity when it changes state, or that mass is lost when a gas is produced. This is like the 2025 board examiner observation that some candidates confused categories, such as amphoteric oxides with basic or neutral oxides, because they did not separate the properties clearly. In melting or boiling, the substance remains the same. Ice, water, and steam are all H2O. During a chemical reaction in a closed system, the total mass before and after is the same.
misconceptions.correction: Remind yourself that a change of state is a physical change, while a reaction with new products is a chemical change. In both cases, the particles themselves are conserved, and so is their mass.

diagnosticQuestions.question: State the main postulates of the kinetic theory of matter.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: The main postulates of the kinetic theory of matter are that all matter is made up of a very large number of tiny particles, which may be atoms or molecules. These particles are in a state of continuous, random motion. The average kinetic energy of these particles is directly related to the temperature of the substance, which means that as the temperature rises, the particles move faster. There are spaces between the particles, and these spaces are smallest in solids, larger in liquids, and largest in gases. There are forces of attraction between the particles; these forces are strongest in solids, weaker in liquids, and weakest in gases. Finally, the particles collide with one another and with the walls of their container, and these collisions help to explain the pressure exerted by gases and the changes of state that occur when energy is added or removed. A correct answer must include all these points because the postulates work together. If any one is left out, the explanation of why solids hold their shape, why liquids flow, and why gases spread out will be incomplete.

diagnosticQuestions.question: Use the kinetic theory to explain why a solid melts when it is heated.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: When a solid is heated, heat energy is transferred to the particles that make up the solid. Because the temperature of the solid increases, the kinetic energy of the particles also increases. In a solid, the particles are already arranged very close to one another and are held in fixed positions by strong forces of inter particle attraction. At first, the particles simply vibrate more and more quickly about their fixed positions. However, as more and more heat is supplied, the particles vibrate so violently that the attractive forces can no longer hold them in their fixed positions. The particles begin to break free from the rigid arrangement and move about more freely, although they remain close to one another. At this point, the solid has melted and become a liquid. The change from solid to liquid is called melting. Throughout the process, the particles themselves are the same; only their arrangement and motion have changed. This shows how the three ideas of particle motion, inter particle space, and inter particle attraction work together to explain a change of state.

diagnosticQuestions.question: "A student says that when a candle burns, the wax disappears, so mass must have been destroyed." Evaluate this statement using the law of conservation of mass.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: This statement is incorrect when it is applied to the complete system, but it contains a partial observation that can be explained by the law of conservation of mass. When a candle burns, the solid wax melts and then reacts with oxygen from the air. The products of this reaction include carbon dioxide gas and water vapour, which are not easily visible and which mix with the surrounding air. Because the gaseous products escape into the atmosphere, the mass of the candle itself seems to decrease. However, if the candle and the air around it were placed inside a closed container and weighed before and after burning, the total mass would remain the same. This is because the law of conservation of mass states that mass is neither created nor destroyed in an ordinary chemical reaction. The total mass of the reactants, which are wax and oxygen, is equal to the total mass of the products, which include carbon dioxide and water vapour. The error in the student's statement is the belief that the wax has simply disappeared. In fact, it has been chemically changed into other substances that have spread into the air. If we only look at the solid candle, we are not measuring the complete system. A correct understanding requires us to consider all the reactants and all the products, including invisible gases. Therefore, the statement is wrong because it ignores the oxygen that took part in the reaction and the gaseous products that were formed, and because it does not measure the total mass of the closed system.

diagnosticQuestions.question: A teacher performs a reaction between barium chloride solution and sodium sulphate solution in a closed conical flask. The total mass before the reaction is 125 g. Predict the total mass after the reaction, and explain your answer using the law of conservation of mass. Also name the reactants and the products.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: The total mass after the reaction will still be 125 g. This is because the reaction is taking place in a closed conical flask, which means no substance can enter or leave the system. According to the law of conservation of mass, the total mass of the reactants is equal to the total mass of the products. The reactants in this reaction are barium chloride, BaCl2, and sodium sulphate, Na2SO4. When their solutions are mixed, a double displacement reaction takes place. The barium ions combine with the sulphate ions to form a white precipitate of barium sulphate, BaSO4. The sodium ions combine with the chloride ions to remain in solution as sodium chloride, NaCl. Since the reaction is in a closed flask, the precipitate, the solution, and any vapour produced are all still inside. Therefore, the mass measured after the reaction is exactly the same as the mass measured before. This is a classic classroom demonstration of the law of conservation of mass, and it shows that a chemical change is simply a rearrangement of particles, not a loss of mass.

diagnosticQuestions.question: Imagine you are a science communicator creating a short comic strip for Class 7 students that explains how adding heat energy changes a solid block of ice in Shimla into water and then into steam. Describe the three frames of your comic strip and the captions you would write.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: Frame one would show a solid block of ice on a snowy roof in Shimla. The particles inside the ice are drawn as small circles packed closely together in a neat, regular pattern, with springs between them to show strong inter particle attraction. The caption reads: "In ice, water particles are close together and strongly attracted. They can only vibrate in fixed positions." Frame two would show the ice beginning to melt as the morning sun adds heat energy. Arrows representing heat are shown entering the ice. The particles are now drawn with squiggly lines to show faster vibration, and a few have broken away from the rigid pattern to move more freely. The space between them has slightly increased. The caption reads: "Heat gives the particles more energy. They vibrate faster and the attraction can no longer hold them in fixed places. The ice melts into water." Frame three would show the water boiling in a pot over a fire. The particles are now drawn far apart, moving rapidly in all directions and colliding with each other and the walls of the pot. Some particles are shown escaping as steam into the air. The caption reads: "More heat makes the particles move very fast. They overcome the attraction completely and spread far apart as steam. Same water molecules, different arrangement." This comic strip uses the kinetic theory to show that adding heat changes motion and arrangement, not the identity of the particles.

masteryCriteria: Can state the three main points of kinetic theory (particles are always moving, higher temperature means faster movement, particles attract each other); can explain why solids have fixed shape (particles vibrate in place), liquids flow (particles slide past each other), and gases spread out (particles move freely).

title: Carbon compounds - basics
subject: chem
definition:
Carbon compounds are substances in which carbon is chemically combined with other elements. In this node we focus on the two simplest gaseous oxides of carbon--carbon dioxide, CO2, and carbon monoxide, CO--and learn how each is prepared, what properties it shows, and why it matters.

Carbon dioxide is prepared in the school laboratory by the action of a dilute acid on a metal carbonate. The most common reactants are marble chips, which are mainly calcium carbonate (CaCO3), and dilute hydrochloric acid (HCl). A brisk effervescence occurs as bubbles of carbon dioxide are set free. The gas is collected by upward displacement of air because it is heavier than air; it is not collected over water because it dissolves to some extent and forms carbonic acid. Sodium carbonate (Na2CO3) may also be used, though the reaction is faster and less easy to control. The balanced reaction is CaCO3 + 2HCl -> CaCl2 + H2O + CO2.

Physically, carbon dioxide is a colourless, odourless gas. It does not burn and it does not support ordinary combustion, although a few very reactive metals such as magnesium can burn in it. Chemically it is acidic: it turns moist blue litmus red because it dissolves in water to form carbonic acid (H2CO3). When carbon dioxide is bubbled through lime water, a clear solution of calcium hydroxide, a white precipitate of calcium carbonate is produced and the liquid turns milky. If carbon dioxide is passed for a longer time, the precipitate dissolves to form soluble calcium bicarbonate, so the milkiness disappears. This two-stage change is a standard test for the gas.

Carbon monoxide is the other common oxide of carbon. It is a colourless, odourless and highly poisonous gas. It is prepared in the laboratory by passing carbon dioxide over heated carbon: CO2 + C -> 2CO. Industrially, it is formed by the incomplete combustion of carbon or carbon compounds. Unlike carbon dioxide, carbon monoxide is a strong reducing agent. In the extraction of iron in a blast furnace, it reduces iron(III) oxide to iron while being oxidised to carbon dioxide. This makes it very valuable in the iron and steel industry. However, when inhaled, carbon monoxide binds strongly to haemoglobin to form carboxyhaemoglobin, reducing the blood's ability to carry oxygen and causing asphyxia. Therefore carbon monoxide must always be handled with care.
eli5: Carbon makes two special invisible airs. Carbon dioxide is the fizz we get when marble and a weak acid mix; it is heavier than air, turns blue paper red, and makes lime water milky. Carbon monoxide is a dangerous gas from partly burning things such as wood or fuel; it helps factories pull iron from rocks, but if you breathe it, it blocks oxygen in your blood and stops your body from breathing properly.

misconceptions.belief: Carbon dioxide is collected over water or by downward displacement of air. This is a common error. board examiners have recommended that teachers explain when to use upward, downward or water displacement. CO2 is denser than air, so it is collected by upward displacement of air; it is not collected over water because it dissolves in water and forms carbonic acid.

The correct laboratory acid for preparing CO2 from marble is concentrated sulphuric acid. This mistake appears in exam guidance where candidates wrote the wrong reagent. The correct reactant is dilute hydrochloric acid (HCl). Concentrated sulphuric acid is a dehydrating agent used in other reactions, and dilute sulphuric acid would form an insoluble layer of calcium sulphate on marble and stop the reaction.

Because carbon dioxide and carbon monoxide are both oxides of carbon, they have similar effects on the body. This is wrong. Carbon dioxide is only mildly acidic and not poisonous at ordinary levels; carbon monoxide is highly toxic, binds to haemoglobin and causes asphyxia. They also differ chemically: CO2 is acidic, while CO is a strong reducing agent in iron extraction.

diagnosticQuestions.question: Describe the laboratory preparation of carbon dioxide from marble and dilute hydrochloric acid, and explain why the gas is collected by upward displacement of air.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: Carbon dioxide is prepared in the laboratory by reacting a metal carbonate with a dilute acid. Marble chips, which are mainly calcium carbonate (CaCO3), are placed in a flask or a Woulfe bottle. Dilute hydrochloric acid (HCl) is poured through a thistle funnel. A brisk effervescence is observed as carbon dioxide gas is given off. The balanced chemical equation is CaCO3 + 2HCl -> CaCl2 + H2O + CO2. The gas is collected in a gas jar by upward displacement of air. This method is chosen because the relative molecular mass of carbon dioxide is 44, which is much greater than the average molecular mass of air (about 29). Therefore carbon dioxide is denser than air and sinks to the bottom of the jar, pushing the lighter air out through the mouth at the top. The gas is not collected over water because it dissolves in water to form carbonic acid, which would lead to loss of the gas and an incorrect result.

diagnosticQuestions.question: Carbon dioxide is passed slowly through lime water and then for a longer time. Describe the changes you would observe and explain the chemistry behind each change.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: Lime water is a clear, colourless solution of calcium hydroxide in water. When carbon dioxide is first bubbled through it, a white precipitate of calcium carbonate is formed. The insoluble calcium carbonate particles make the clear liquid look milky. The reaction can be written as Ca(OH)2 + CO2 -> CaCO3 + H2O. If carbon dioxide is passed for a longer time, the white precipitate dissolves and the solution becomes clear again. This happens because calcium carbonate reacts with more carbon dioxide and water to form soluble calcium bicarbonate: CaCO3 + CO2 + H2O -> Ca(HCO3)2. The milkiness therefore first appears and then disappears. This two-stage test is used as a confirmatory test for carbon dioxide. A student who only mentions the milky appearance has given an incomplete answer; both the formation and the disappearance of the precipitate must be explained.

diagnosticQuestions.question: "Carbon dioxide and carbon monoxide are both oxides of carbon, so they have the same physical and chemical properties and can be handled in the same way." Evaluate this statement.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: This statement is only partly correct and is largely misleading. It is true that both carbon dioxide and carbon monoxide are oxides of carbon and that both are colourless, odourless gases. However, they differ greatly in their physical and chemical behaviour. Carbon dioxide is acidic in nature: it turns blue litmus red, dissolves in water to form carbonic acid, and is heavier than air. Carbon monoxide is neutral, only slightly soluble in water, burns with a blue flame and is not acidic. Chemically, carbon dioxide does not support combustion in ordinary cases, whereas carbon monoxide is a strong reducing agent and is used to reduce iron(III) oxide to iron in the blast furnace. The two gases also differ sharply in their effect on living things. Carbon dioxide is not poisonous at the concentrations usually found around us, although too much of it can cause suffocation by displacing oxygen. Carbon monoxide, on the other hand, is highly toxic even in small amounts because it binds to haemoglobin to form carboxyhaemoglobin, preventing oxygen from being carried in the blood and causing asphyxia. Because of these differences, they cannot be handled in the same way. Carbon dioxide can be safely prepared and demonstrated in the laboratory, while carbon monoxide must be produced in a fume cupboard or with proper ventilation and must never be inhaled. Therefore the statement is false and each oxide must be treated as a distinct substance.

diagnosticQuestions.question: A student is asked to demonstrate, in the laboratory, that the gas produced from marble chips and dilute HCl is carbon dioxide. Describe the practical steps, the expected observations, and the conclusions.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: The student should set up the apparatus as follows. Place a few marble chips, which are calcium carbonate, in a flask fitted with a thistle funnel and a delivery tube. Pour dilute hydrochloric acid through the thistle funnel so that it comes into contact with the marble. A brisk effervescence shows that a gas is being produced. Connect the delivery tube to an inverted gas jar placed mouth upward in a trough or on a shelf, and collect the gas by upward displacement of air. Once a jar is full, remove the tube, cover the jar with a glass plate, and carry out three tests. First, bring a burning splint near the mouth of the jar; the splint should be extinguished, showing that the gas does not support combustion. Second, place a piece of blue litmus paper that has been moistened with water into the jar; it turns red, showing that the gas is acidic. Third, bubble the gas through fresh lime water; the lime water first turns milky due to the formation of a white precipitate of calcium carbonate, and on passing more gas the milkiness disappears because soluble calcium bicarbonate is formed. All three observations together confirm that the gas produced is carbon dioxide.

diagnosticQuestions.question: Design a short safety poster for a family that uses a kerosene stove in a small, poorly ventilated kitchen. Your poster should explain how carbon monoxide forms and how to prevent poisoning.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: The poster should have a bold heading such as "Carbon Monoxide Can Kill--Keep Your Kitchen Safe." The first section should explain, in simple language, that kerosene contains carbon and that when it burns with plenty of air it forms carbon dioxide, which is not poisonous. When the air supply is poor, the fuel does not burn completely and produces carbon monoxide, an invisible, odourless gas that can cause asphyxia. The second section should list clear safety rules: always keep a window or vent open, use an exhaust fan when cooking, make sure the burner flame is blue rather than yellow or orange, never block air vents, do not use the stove to heat the room at night, and leave the kitchen immediately if anyone feels dizzy or has a headache. A small illustration should show a blue flame for complete combustion and a yellow flame for incomplete combustion. The final section should give the first-aid step: move the person to fresh air at once and call for medical help. The poster should end with the warning: "Carbon monoxide has no smell--only good ventilation can keep you safe."

masteryCriteria: Can state that carbon forms covalent bonds by sharing electrons (tetravalent: forms 4 bonds); can name three simple carbon compounds (CO2, CH4, CaCO3); can classify carbon compounds as organic (CH4, C2H5OH) or inorganic (CO2, CaCO3); can state two reasons why carbon forms many compounds (catenation, tetravalency).

title: Physical changes - reversible and irreversible
subject: chem
definition: A physical change is a transformation in which the outward appearance, state, or shape of a substance alters, but no new substance is formed. The same particles remain the same; they are simply rearranged, separated, or packed differently. In Class 7, we move beyond simply recognising physical changes and begin to classify them as reversible or irreversible. A reversible physical change is one in which the original substance can be regained by reversing the conditions. Common examples are the melting of ice, the freezing of water, the dissolution of common salt in water followed by its recovery by evaporation, and the sublimation of camphor, which changes directly from a solid to a gas and can be made to return to a solid by cooling. An irreversible physical change is one in which the original form cannot be restored without using glue or other external help; the substance is still the same, but its shape or size is permanently altered. Examples are cutting a sheet of paper, breaking a glass tumbler, tearing cloth, or bursting a balloon. The key to understanding reversibility is the idea of particle arrangement. In reversible changes, particles can move back to their original positions because their attractions remain unchanged. In irreversible changes such as cutting or breaking, the particles are physically separated so far apart, or the structure is so disrupted, that the original shape cannot be reformed by a simple change of conditions. Sublimation is special: the solid particles escape straight into the gas state and can settle back again as a solid, which is why it is counted as a reversible physical change. It is important to keep physical changes separate from chemical changes. Rusting of iron, for example, is not a physical change at all; it is a chemical change because a new substance, rust, is formed. The distinction between physical and chemical changes depends on whether a new substance is produced, while the distinction between reversible and irreversible physical changes depends on whether the original state or shape can be recovered by ordinary physical means.
eli5: A physical change is when something looks different but is still the same stuff. Melting ice is like water putting on a new outfit; you can freeze it back. Cutting paper is like tearing a picture; the pieces are still paper, but you cannot stick them back perfectly. So some changes can be undone, and some cannot.

diagnosticQuestions.question: What is a physical change? Classify physical changes into reversible and irreversible types and give two examples of each type.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: A physical change is a change in which the appearance, shape, or state of a substance alters but no new substance is formed. The particles of the substance remain the same and can usually be recognised by simple tests. Physical changes can be divided into reversible and irreversible types. Reversible physical changes are changes in which the original substance can be regained by reversing the conditions. The melting of ice into water and its refreezing is a classic example, because the water particles can return to the solid lattice when the temperature is lowered. Another example is the sublimation of camphor, which changes directly from a solid to a gas and can be converted back into a solid when the vapour is cooled. A third example is the dissolution of common salt in water, which is reversible because the water can be evaporated to recover the salt. Irreversible physical changes are changes in which the original form cannot be restored without using an external agent such as glue or stitching. Cutting a sheet of paper is an irreversible physical change because the pieces are still paper, but the single sheet cannot be restored just by changing conditions. Breaking a glass tumbler is another example, because the shards cannot rejoin themselves into the original tumbler. In every case, the key point is that the substance itself remains the same; only the state, shape, or size is altered.

diagnosticQuestions.question: Why is the melting of ice a reversible physical change while cutting a sheet of paper is an irreversible physical change? Explain using the idea of particle arrangement.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: The melting of ice is reversible because the water particles in ice are held in a fixed, orderly arrangement by strong forces of attraction. When heat is supplied, the particles gain kinetic energy, vibrate more vigorously, and finally break away from their fixed positions, producing liquid water. Importantly, the particles are still water particles; they have not changed into anything new. If the liquid water is cooled, the particles lose kinetic energy, slow down, and settle back into the regular lattice of ice. The original arrangement can be restored simply by reversing the temperature. In contrast, when a sheet of paper is cut, the long cellulose fibres and the tiny particles making up the paper are physically separated and pushed apart. The pieces are still paper, so it is a physical change, but the separated particles and fibres cannot move back into their original, continuous arrangement on their own. No change of temperature, pressure, or simple physical treatment will make the cut disappear. That is why cutting is an irreversible physical change. The difference, therefore, lies in whether the particles can return to their original positions: in melting ice they can, but in cutting paper they cannot.

diagnosticQuestions.question: A student says, "All physical changes are reversible, and all changes that cannot be reversed are chemical changes." Evaluate this statement carefully, giving a balanced argument and clear examples.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: This statement is only partly true and is largely incorrect as a general rule. It confuses three different ideas: physical change, reversibility, and chemical change. To evaluate it properly, we must consider each part separately. The first part claims that all physical changes are reversible. This is false. Many physical changes are indeed reversible, such as the melting of ice, the freezing of water, the dissolution and recovery of salt, and the sublimation of camphor. In each of these cases, the same substance can be restored by reversing the conditions because the particles can return to their original arrangement. However, some physical changes are irreversible. Cutting paper, breaking glass, tearing cloth, and bursting a balloon are all physical changes because no new substance is formed, but they cannot be undone by ordinary physical means. The original shape or size is permanently lost. Therefore, the first part of the statement is wrong because physical changes can be either reversible or irreversible. The second part claims that all irreversible changes are chemical changes. This is also false. A chemical change is defined by the formation of a new substance, not by the inability to reverse the change. Rusting of iron is a chemical change and is difficult to reverse, but burning magnesium or cooking an egg are also chemical changes that are not usually reversed. More importantly, many irreversible changes are not chemical at all. Breaking a glass tumbler is irreversible, yet the glass particles are still the same; it is an irreversible physical change. The statement fails to notice that irreversibility can apply to both physical and chemical changes, and that the real test for a chemical change is the production of a new substance, not the difficulty of reversing the process. In a balanced conclusion, we can say that while many reversible changes are physical and many chemical changes are difficult to reverse, the reverse is not automatically true. We must classify a change first by asking whether a new substance is formed, and only then ask whether the original form can be recovered.

diagnosticQuestions.question: In a science fair activity, a Class 7 student performs three actions: (a) drops an ice cube into a bowl of warm water, (b) breaks a glass tumbler by accident, and (c) warms a small piece of camphor until it disappears. Classify each change as reversible or irreversible, and explain whether any of these is a chemical change.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: In action (a), the ice cube melts into liquid water because the water particles gain heat energy, vibrate faster, and break away from their fixed positions in the ice crystal. This is a reversible physical change because the liquid water can be placed in a freezer and converted back into ice. The same water particles are still present, and no new substance has formed. In action (b), the glass tumbler breaks into many pieces. This is an irreversible physical change because the pieces are still glass, so no new substance is formed, but the original tumbler cannot be restored without the use of an adhesive. The particles of glass have been separated in a way that cannot be undone by simply changing temperature or pressure. In action (c), the camphor warms and sublimes, changing directly from a solid to a gas. The camphor vapour can be cooled on a cold surface to collect solid camphor again. This is a reversible physical change. None of the three is a chemical change, because in each case the substance remains the same: water remains water, glass remains glass, and camphor remains camphor. A chemical change would require the formation of a new substance, such as rust on iron or ash from burning paper.

diagnosticQuestions.question: Design a simple home or classroom experiment to demonstrate one reversible physical change and one irreversible physical change. List the materials, the steps, the observations you expect, and the conclusion you will draw.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: The experiment can be done on a kitchen table using materials that are easy to find. For the reversible physical change, take two small glass tumblers, a teaspoon of common salt, about fifty millilitres of water, and a small saucer or shallow dish. First, fill one tumbler with water and add the salt. Stir until the salt disappears. This shows dissolution, which is a physical change because the salt particles spread through the water but are still salt. Next, pour the salt water into the saucer and leave it on a warm window-sill for a day, or warm it very gently with the help of an adult. Observe that the water slowly disappears and white, salty crystals remain in the saucer. Conclude that dissolution of salt is a reversible physical change because the original salt can be recovered by evaporating the water. For the irreversible physical change, take a sheet of waste paper and a pair of scissors. Measure the length and width of the sheet and then cut it into several small pieces. Observe that each piece is still paper, so no new substance has formed. Try to make the sheet whole again without using glue or tape. You will find that the original sheet cannot be restored. Conclude that cutting paper is an irreversible physical change because the original shape cannot be recovered by ordinary physical means. The overall lesson is that a physical change may be reversible or irreversible, and the test is whether the original substance and shape can be regained.

masteryCriteria: Can define reversible physical changes (can be undone: melting ice, dissolving salt) and irreversible physical changes (cannot be undone: tearing paper, breaking glass); can classify five physical changes as reversible or irreversible; can explain why dissolving is reversible but breaking is not.

title: Chemical changes - characteristics
subject: chem
definition: A chemical change is a process in which one or more substances are converted into entirely new substances that have different properties from the original substances. Unlike a physical change, where only the state, size, or shape of a substance is altered, a chemical change produces a new substance whose chemical composition and properties are fundamentally different from the substances that formed it. The characteristics of a chemical change are the observable signs that tell us that a new substance has been formed. These characteristics include the formation of a new substance, a change in colour, the evolution of a gas, and a change in energy, which may appear as heat, light, or sound. When milk turns into curd, the creamy white liquid becomes a thick, sour semi-solid because new substances such as lactic acid are formed; this is curdling, and it is a chemical change. When iron objects are left in the open air and rain, they develop a reddish-brown coating called rust, which is a new substance called iron oxide; this is rusting, and it is a chemical change. When eggs rot, the proteins inside them break down and form new substances with a foul smell and a changed colour; this is rotting, and it is a chemical change. In contrast, when ice melts, it changes from a solid to a liquid, but the substance is still water; this is melting, and it is only a physical change. When camphor is heated, it changes directly from a solid to a gas without melting, and the gas can cool back to solid camphor; this is sublimation, and it is also a physical change. The key to differentiation is to look for the formation of a new substance. A physical change may sometimes be irreversible, like tearing a piece of paper, but it does not produce a new substance with different chemical properties. A chemical change, however, is usually irreversible by simple physical means, and it always produces a new substance. Therefore, the characteristics of a chemical change--new substance, colour change, gas evolution, and energy change--help us to distinguish chemical changes from physical changes such as melting and sublimation.
eli5: When something changes into a totally new thing, it is a chemical change. Milk turning into curd, iron turning into rust, and eggs going bad are all chemical changes because a new stuff is made. Melting ice and camphor disappearing into the air are physical changes because the same stuff is still there, just in a different shape or state.

misconceptions.belief: "Any colour change means a chemical change has happened." This is incorrect. A colour change is a sign of a chemical change only when a new substance is formed. For example, rusting of iron shows a colour change because iron becomes iron oxide, which is a new substance. However, mixing blue ink with water changes the colour, but no new substance is formed, so it is a physical change. board examiners repeatedly stress that students must focus on the colour and solubility of the products formed; for rust, the new substance is a reddish-brown solid, and that is why the colour change is meaningful.

"If a change is irreversible, it must be a chemical change." This is incorrect. Many physical changes are also irreversible. When you tear a piece of paper, you cannot put the pieces back together perfectly, but no new substance has been formed; the paper is still paper. A good answer must mention that a chemical change produces a new substance, not merely that it cannot be reversed. The CISCE Common board exam error pattern notes that students often confuse observations with conclusions; practising observation-based questions will help you avoid this mistake.

"Sublimation of camphor is a chemical change because the solid disappears and a gas appears." This is incorrect. During sublimation, solid camphor turns directly into camphor vapour, and when cooled, the vapour returns to solid camphor. The substance is still camphor, so no new substance is formed. It is a physical change. This is similar to the common student error of writing wrong chemical formulas or confusing the name of a substance with its formula; examiners have noticed that some students give the name when the formula is asked, or write an incorrect ratio. Here, the correction is to identify the substance correctly: if the same substance returns after cooling, no new substance has been formed.

diagnosticQuestions.question: List the four main characteristics of a chemical change and give one example from the syllabus for each characteristic.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: The four main characteristics of a chemical change are the formation of a new substance, a change in colour, the evolution of a gas, and a change in energy. The formation of a new substance is shown when milk turns into curd; the curd is a new substance with a different taste, smell, and texture from milk. A change in colour is shown when iron rusts; the silvery-grey metal turns into a reddish-brown powder called rust. The evolution of a gas is shown when an egg rots; gases such as hydrogen sulphide are produced, giving the rotten egg its bad smell. A change in energy is shown when fuel burns; heat and light are released as new substances such as carbon dioxide and water vapour are formed. These four characteristics help us to recognise that a chemical change has taken place, because in each case a new substance with different properties is produced.

diagnosticQuestions.question: Explain why melting of ice is a physical change but rusting of iron is a chemical change, even though both involve a change in appearance.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: Melting of ice is a physical change because only the state of water changes from solid to liquid. The substance remains H_2O in both cases; it is still water. No new substance is formed, and the change can be reversed by freezing the water back into ice. On the other hand, rusting of iron is a chemical change because the iron reacts with oxygen and water in the air to form a new substance called rust, which is chemically iron oxide. Rust is reddish-brown, brittle, and has different properties from the original iron. The colour change from silvery-grey to reddish-brown is not just a surface change; it shows that a new substance has been produced. Rusting cannot be reversed simply by physical means such as cooling or pressing. Therefore, both changes may look different, but melting of ice is physical because no new substance is formed, while rusting is chemical because a new substance is formed.

diagnosticQuestions.question: A student says, "Sublimation of camphor is a chemical change because white solid camphor disappears and a gas is produced." Evaluate this statement and decide whether you agree or disagree.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: I disagree with the statement. Sublimation of camphor is a physical change, not a chemical change. The student has observed correctly that the white solid disappears and a gas appears, but the important question is whether a new substance has been formed. During sublimation, solid camphor changes directly into camphor vapour without passing through the liquid state. However, the vapour is still camphor; the substance has not changed chemically. If the vapour is cooled, it condenses back into solid camphor. This reversibility shows that no new substance has been formed. The student has confused a change of state with a chemical change. A chemical change, such as rusting of iron or curdling of milk, produces a new substance with different chemical properties that cannot be easily recovered. In sublimation, the camphor can be recovered unchanged, so it is a physical change. The student should look for evidence of a new substance, such as a colour change that cannot be reversed, gas evolution that produces a different substance, or an energy change that accompanies the formation of new products. In this case, none of these are present. The statement is therefore incorrect, but the student should be praised for making a careful observation; the next step is to test whether the original substance can be recovered.

diagnosticQuestions.question: Your grandmother stores camphor tablets in a cupboard, and after a few months the tablets have become smaller but a white solid has appeared on the cooler shelf above them. She asks you whether this is a chemical change. What will you tell her, and how will you prove it?
diagnosticQuestions.answer: I will tell her that this is a physical change, not a chemical change. The camphor tablets have become smaller because of sublimation: the solid camphor has changed directly into camphor vapour. The white solid on the cooler shelf above is the same camphor that has cooled and turned back into a solid. I can prove this by collecting the white solid and checking its properties. If it is still camphor, it will have the same strong smell, the same white colour, and the same ability to sublimate when heated. I could also weigh the camphor before and after; if the total mass is almost the same and the substance has simply moved from one place to another, no new substance has been formed. Since the same substance is still present, the change is physical. This is different from rusting, where the original iron cannot be recovered simply by cooling or collecting the rust.

diagnosticQuestions.question: Design a simple home experiment to show that curdling of milk is a chemical change and not a physical change. List the materials, the steps, and the observations that would support your conclusion.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: Materials needed: fresh milk in a small bowl, a few spoonfuls of curd or lemon juice, a spoon, a clean cloth or filter, and two small bowls. Steps: 1. Pour about half a cup of fresh milk into a bowl and observe its colour, smell, and state. 2. Add one spoonful of curd or a few drops of lemon juice to the milk and stir gently. 3. Leave the bowl at room temperature for a few hours. 4. After a few hours, observe the milk again. 5. Try to filter the mixture using a clean cloth or filter and see whether you can get the original milk back. Observations: The milk will become thick and lumpy, its smell will change from mildly sweet to sour, and its colour may appear slightly yellowish. When you filter it, you will not get back the original smooth milk; instead, you will get a thick curd and a watery liquid called whey. Conclusion: The curd is a new substance with a different taste, smell, and texture from the original milk. Because a new substance has been formed and the original milk cannot be recovered, curdling of milk is a chemical change. This experiment shows that the characteristics of a chemical change--new substance, colour change, and energy change in the form of slight warmth--are present, so it cannot be a physical change.

masteryCriteria: Can state four characteristics of a chemical change (new substance formed, irreversible, energy change, colour/gas/precipitate change); can identify a chemical change from given observations (e.g., burning candle, rusting iron); can distinguish chemical from physical changes using two tests.

title: Chemical reactions in daily life
subject: chem
definition: A chemical reaction in daily life is an event in which one or more starting substances are converted into one or more new substances that have different properties from the materials you began with. You already know, from earlier classes, that a physical change is usually reversible and does not create a new substance: melting ice, tearing paper, or dissolving sugar in lemonade may alter the size, shape, or state of a material, but the material itself stays the same. In a chemical change, the particles rearrange, new bonds are formed, and an entirely new substance is produced. The Class 7 syllabus now asks you to identify and classify these changes in the world around you. Rusting is the slow reaction of iron with oxygen and water from the air to form hydrated iron(III) oxide, the reddish-brown, flaky substance that collects on an old gate or a bicycle left in the rain. Cooking is the heat-driven chemical change of dough, rice, vegetables, or meat into softer, often brown and aromatic products whose taste, smell, colour, and structure are completely different from the raw starting materials. Burning is a rapid reaction between a fuel and oxygen that releases heat and light and forms new substances such as carbon dioxide, water vapour, and ash. Digestion is the series of chemical reactions in the body that converts food such as chapati, dal, fruit, eggs, and milk into simpler substances that can be absorbed and used for energy. Classification of these changes means sorting daily events into physical and chemical change groups. The key diagnostic characteristics are a change in colour, the evolution of a gas, a change in energy such as heat or light being produced or absorbed, the formation of an insoluble solid, and the fact that the original substance cannot be brought back by simple physical means. When a change is irreversible and produces a new substance, it is a chemical reaction. When the original substance can be recovered unchanged, it is a physical change. Terms such as curd, fuel, energy, and irreversible are not just vocabulary items; they are the signposts that help you read the chemistry hidden in your kitchen, garden, and body.
eli5: Sometimes things around you only change their shape or size, like ice melting into water. That is a physical change. Other times, one thing turns into a completely new thing, like milk becoming sour curd or a matchstick turning into ash and smoke. That is a chemical change, also called a chemical reaction. You can tell it happened because the new thing looks, smells, or feels different and you cannot change it back.

misconceptions.belief: Writing the name of the new substance instead of describing the evidence. The board examiner observation for the 2020 paper noted that several candidates wrote the reactions or named the product instead of writing the observations. In the same way, a Class 7 learner may answer that rusting is a chemical change because rust is formed. The correction is to describe the observable evidence: the colour changes from silver-grey to reddish-brown, the surface becomes rough and flaky, and the original iron cannot be recovered. Naming the product is not enough; the characteristics that reveal the new substance are what earn marks.

Confusing one kind of change with another because of a surface similarity. The 2019 examiner observation about medicines noted that many candidates, instead of writing antipyretics, wrote analgesics, showing that students often confuse two related categories. In Class 7, a similar error occurs when students think that anything hot is a chemical change. Boiling water, for example, is hot and produces bubbles of steam, but the water can be cooled back to liquid water. That is a physical change. Burning fuel is also hot, but the fuel turns into new substances such as carbon dioxide and ash, so it is a chemical change. The correction is to ask not whether heat is present, but whether a new, irreversible substance has formed.

Choosing the wrong reagent or the wrong example. The 2020 paper noted that a number of candidates chose the incorrect reagent and could not write the correct observations. In this topic, a student may choose curdling of milk as a physical change because the milk still looks white. The correction is to use several characteristics together: curd has a sour smell, a thick texture, a different taste, and the original milk cannot be recovered. It is, therefore, a chemical change. Always check more than one characteristic before deciding.

diagnosticQuestions.question: Define a chemical change and list the main characteristics that help you decide whether an everyday event is a chemical reaction rather than a physical change.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: A chemical change, also called a chemical reaction, is a process in which one or more substances are converted into one or more new substances that have different properties from the original substances. The main characteristics that help you decide whether a change is chemical include a change in colour, the evolution of a gas, a change in energy such as heat or light being given out or taken in, the formation of a new solid or an insoluble substance, and the fact that the change is usually irreversible by simple physical means. For example, when a matchstick burns, the wood changes from brown to black and ash, heat and light are released, and the gases that rise into the air are new substances. If you tried to put the matchstick back together, you could not get the original wood back. Similarly, when milk turns into curd, the colour and texture change, a sour smell and taste appear, and the milk cannot be stirred back into its original form. These characteristics work like a checklist: if several of them appear together, you can confidently say that a chemical reaction has taken place in daily life.

diagnosticQuestions.question: A piece of bread is left in a damp kitchen in a coastal city like Kochi. After two weeks, it is covered with green and grey spots. Explain whether this is a physical change or a chemical change, and describe the evidence that a new substance has formed.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: The bread turning green and grey is a chemical change, not a physical change. A physical change, such as cutting the bread into slices or drying it in the sun, does not create a new substance and can usually be reversed. When the bread is left in the damp kitchen, tiny living things called fungi grow on it and break down the bread into new substances. The evidence that a new substance has formed is clear: the colour changes from its original cream or brown to patches of green, grey, or black; a different smell appears, often a musty or sour one; the texture becomes soft or slimy; and the original bread cannot be made fresh again by any simple method. If you tried to remove the spots, you would still not have the original piece of bread back. These changes in colour, smell, texture, and irreversibility are the characteristics of a chemical reaction. Therefore, the rotting of bread is a chemical change that takes place in daily life.

diagnosticQuestions.question: A student says, "Cooking rice and ironing a cotton shirt are both chemical changes because the materials look different after the process." Evaluate this statement and give a balanced argument.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: This statement is only partly correct, because only one of the two processes is a chemical change. Cooking rice is a chemical change. The raw grain is hard, dry, and tasteless, but after boiling it absorbs water, becomes soft and white, and has a cooked smell and taste. New substances are formed when the heat breaks down some of the starch and protein in the grain. The cooked rice cannot be turned back into the raw grain by cooling or pressing it, so the change is irreversible. On the other hand, ironing a cotton shirt is not a chemical change. The heat from the iron may remove moisture and smooth out the cloth, but the cotton itself remains cotton. If the shirt is crumpled again or sprinkled with water, it returns to a wrinkled or damp state, but the cotton does not become a new substance. The change in appearance is only temporary and reversible, so it is a physical change. The student's mistake is to think that every change in appearance is a chemical change. A balanced view is that appearance can change in both physical and chemical processes. The deciding factors are whether a new substance is formed and whether the change is reversible. The shirt looks different because of smoothing and loss of water, but no new substance is formed; the rice looks and tastes different because new substances are formed and the process is irreversible. Therefore, the statement is incorrect if applied to both examples together, though it is correct when applied only to cooking.

diagnosticQuestions.question: You are given four events from a day in an Indian home: (i) a block of ice is placed in a glass of warm nimbu pani and melts, (ii) a gas stove is lit to make tea, (iii) milk is boiled and then cooled to set into curd, and (iv) a piece of paper is torn into small bits. Classify each as a physical or chemical change and justify your answer using at least one characteristic of a chemical change.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: In the first event, the ice melting in the nimbu pani is a physical change. The solid water turns into liquid water, but the substance is still water. It can be frozen again, so the change is reversible and no new substance is formed. In the second event, lighting the gas stove is a chemical change. The fuel, which is mainly methane, reacts with oxygen to produce carbon dioxide and water vapour, and the reaction gives out heat and light. The fuel is no longer fuel, and a new substance such as carbon dioxide is formed. In the third event, setting curd from milk is a chemical change. The warm milk, after a small amount of curd is added, turns into a thick, sour, white substance with a different smell and taste. The milk has become a new substance, and the original milk cannot be recovered by simple means. In the fourth event, tearing a paper into small bits is a physical change. The paper is divided into smaller pieces, but each piece is still paper. The pieces can be put together or left as they are, but no new substance is formed. The key test is always the same: is a new substance formed, and can the change be reversed easily?

diagnosticQuestions.question: Design a simple classroom activity that demonstrates rusting as a chemical change. Include the materials, the steps, the expected observations, and the conclusion you would draw.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: A simple classroom activity to show rusting as a chemical change needs a few clean iron nails, two small glass jars, tap water, and a little cooking oil. First, wash two iron nails with a dry cloth so that the surface is bright and clean. Place one nail in a dry jar, leaving it exposed only to air. Place the second nail in a jar that is half-filled with tap water, and cover the surface of the water with a thin layer of oil so that the water cannot easily evaporate. Leave both jars undisturbed for five to seven days in the classroom. Observe the nails each day. In the jar with water, the nail will slowly develop a reddish-brown coating, especially near the water line, and the water may turn slightly brown. In the dry jar, the nail may remain almost unchanged or may show only a very small amount of colour change. The expected observation is that the wet nail forms rust while the dry nail does not, showing that rusting needs both iron, water, and oxygen from the air. The conclusion is that rust is a new substance because it has a different colour, a different texture, and it cannot be rubbed off to reveal the original shiny iron underneath. The nail cannot be turned back into its original state by simple drying or pressing, so rusting is a chemical change and an example of a chemical reaction in daily life.

masteryCriteria: Can name three chemical reactions in daily life (rusting of iron, burning of fuel, cooking of food, digestion, fermentation); can explain why rusting is a chemical change (new substance iron oxide formed); can state one way to prevent rusting (painting, galvanising, oiling).

title: Compounds - types and formation
subject: chem
definition:
A compound is a pure substance that is formed when two or more different elements combine chemically in a fixed ratio by mass. Once the elements have joined, the resulting substance has properties that are quite different from the properties of the individual elements that made it.
