For example, sodium is a soft, highly reactive metal that fizzles and skates on water, chlorine is a greenish, poisonous gas, and yet the compound sodium chloride is the harmless, white crystalline solid we use every day as table salt. This difference in properties is one of the best proofs that a chemical combination has taken place.
The force that holds the atoms together in a compound is called a chemical bond, and the process by which the compound is made is called compound formation. In Class 6 you learned that a compound is always formed by the chemical combination of elements in fixed proportions. In Class 7 we take the next step and look at the two main ways in which this chemical combination can occur: ionic bonding and covalent bonding. The type of bonding depends on the kinds of elements that are reacting. If a metal combines with a non-metal, the metal loses one or more electrons and the non-metal gains them. The positive metal ion and the negative non-metal ion are then attracted to each other by a strong electrostatic force, and this is called an ionic bond. Sodium chloride is the classic example of an ionic compound: sodium transfers an electron to chlorine, turning sodium into a sodium ion and chlorine into a chloride ion, and the two ions are held together by ionic bonding.
If two non-metal atoms combine, neither of them can easily give away electrons completely. Instead, the atoms share one or more pairs of electrons between them, and this is called a covalent bond. Water is a covalent compound in which each hydrogen atom shares an electron pair with the oxygen atom. Carbon dioxide is another covalent compound in which a carbon atom shares electrons with two oxygen atoms. In covalent bonding the atoms remain neutral overall, but the shared electrons hold them together strongly. It is important to remember that a compound is not simply a mixture. In a mixture, such as sand and salt, the substances are physically mixed and can usually be separated by physical methods such as filtration, evaporation or decantation, which you already studied in Class 5. In a compound, the elements are joined by chemical bonds and can only be separated by chemical means. The ratio of the elements in a compound is always fixed, but the ratio in a mixture can vary. Reactant elements are the starting substances that combine to form the compound, and the compound itself is the product of that chemical combination.
eli5: A compound is made when different elements join together like building blocks. Sometimes one block gives away marbles, and sometimes two blocks share marbles. Salt is made when sodium gives a tiny particle to chlorine. Water is made when hydrogen and oxygen share tiny particles. A compound is a brand new thing, not just a mix of old things.

diagnosticQuestions.question: Define a compound and state two ways in which a compound is different from a mixture.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: A compound is a pure substance that is formed when two or more different elements combine chemically in a fixed ratio by mass. The elements are held together by chemical bonds, and the resulting compound has properties that are very different from the properties of the original elements. A mixture, on the other hand, is a combination of two or more substances that are not chemically joined. The first important difference is that a compound has a fixed composition by mass, whereas a mixture can have any proportion of its components. For example, water always contains hydrogen and oxygen in the ratio 1:8 by mass, but a mixture of salt and sand can be 1:1, 1:2 or any other ratio. The second important difference is that the components of a compound can only be separated by chemical means, while the components of a mixture can usually be separated by physical methods such as filtration, evaporation or decantation. This is why sea water can be separated into salt and water by evaporation, but water cannot be separated into hydrogen and oxygen by simply boiling it.

diagnosticQuestions.question: Explain why sodium chloride is called an ionic compound, while water is called a covalent compound. Your answer should mention the nature of the elements involved and the way the electrons behave.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: Sodium chloride is called an ionic compound because it is formed by the transfer of an electron from a metal to a non-metal. Sodium is a metal and has one electron in its outermost shell that it can easily give away. Chlorine is a non-metal and has seven electrons in its outermost shell, so it needs one more electron to complete a stable group of eight. When sodium and chlorine combine, the sodium atom transfers its outermost electron to the chlorine atom. The sodium atom becomes a positively charged sodium ion and the chlorine atom becomes a negatively charged chloride ion. These oppositely charged ions attract each other strongly and form an ionic bond. Water, however, is called a covalent compound because it is formed by the sharing of electrons between non-metal atoms. Hydrogen and oxygen are both non-metals. Neither of them wants to give away electrons completely, so each hydrogen atom shares a pair of electrons with the oxygen atom. The shared electrons hold the atoms together, but the atoms remain neutral overall. This kind of bonding, in which electrons are shared rather than transferred, is called covalent bonding. So the nature of the elements determines the type of bond: metal plus non-metal gives ionic, while non-metal plus non-metal gives covalent.

diagnosticQuestions.question: A student says, "All compounds that are formed by sharing of electrons are made of the same element, and all compounds that are formed by the transfer of electrons are made of a metal and a non-metal." Evaluate this statement.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: The student's statement is only partly correct and contains two important mistakes. The second part is correct: compounds formed by the transfer of electrons, which are called ionic compounds, are indeed usually made of a metal and a non-metal. The metal loses electrons to form a positive ion, and the non-metal gains those electrons to form a negative ion. Sodium chloride is a clear example, because sodium is a metal and chlorine is a non-metal. However, the first part is wrong. Compounds that are formed by the sharing of electrons, which are called covalent compounds, are not made of the same element. Covalent compounds are usually made of two or more different non-metal elements. For example, water is a covalent compound made of hydrogen and oxygen, which are different elements, and carbon dioxide is a covalent compound made of carbon and oxygen. Even when a covalent substance is made of only one element, such as chlorine gas Cl2 or hydrogen gas H2, it is technically a molecule rather than a compound, because a compound must contain two or more different elements combined in a fixed ratio. Therefore the student has correctly identified that ionic compounds are formed by electron transfer between a metal and a non-metal, but has incorrectly assumed that all covalent compounds are made of the same element. Covalent compounds are formed by electron sharing, but the sharing usually happens between different non-metal atoms.

diagnosticQuestions.question: You are given the following pairs of reactants: (a) sodium and chlorine, (b) carbon and oxygen, (c) hydrogen and oxygen. For each pair, predict the type of compound that will be formed and explain, in terms of electron transfer or electron sharing, how the bond is made.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: For pair (a), sodium and chlorine, the compound formed is sodium chloride. Sodium is a metal and chlorine is a non-metal, so the bond is ionic. Sodium has one electron in its outermost shell and gives it to chlorine. After the transfer, sodium becomes a sodium ion with a positive charge and chlorine becomes a chloride ion with a negative charge. The strong attraction between these oppositely charged ions holds the ionic compound together. For pair (b), carbon and oxygen, the compound formed is carbon dioxide. Both carbon and oxygen are non-metals, so the bond is covalent. The carbon atom shares electrons with each of the two oxygen atoms, forming double covalent bonds. No electron is transferred completely; the atoms remain neutral and are held together by the shared electron pairs. For pair (c), hydrogen and oxygen, the compound formed is water. Hydrogen and oxygen are both non-metals, so the bond is covalent. Each hydrogen atom shares one pair of electrons with the oxygen atom, giving the familiar H2O molecule. Again, the bonding is by electron sharing, not electron transfer. Thus, by looking at the nature of the reactant elements, we can decide whether the product will be an ionic compound or a covalent compound.

diagnosticQuestions.question: Imagine you have to teach a small child what a covalent compound is. Create a simple analogy to explain the formation of a covalent compound, and then use your analogy to explain why a covalent compound is not the same as a mixture.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: My analogy is a shared blanket on a cold night. Imagine two friends, one named Hydi and one named Oxy, who are both very cold. Neither of them wants to give away their own blanket, but they are happy to share one large blanket between them. When they pull the blanket over both of them, they are held close together and become a single warm group. This is like covalent bonding, in which two non-metal atoms share a pair of electrons instead of one atom giving its electrons to the other. Hydi and Oxy remain two different people, just as hydrogen and oxygen remain two different elements, but the shared blanket holds them together as a team. Now, this is not the same as a mixture. If Hydi had one blanket and Oxy had another, and they simply placed their blankets on the same bed without sharing, they would still each own their own blanket. They could easily be separated. That is like a mixture, in which the different substances are mixed together physically but keep their own properties and can be separated. In the covalent compound, the two friends are now one warm unit, and separating them would be much harder because they are joined by the shared blanket. In the same way, hydrogen and oxygen in water are joined by shared electrons and cannot be separated by simple physical methods.

masteryCriteria: Can classify compounds as acids (HCl, H2SO4), bases (NaOH, KOH), or salts (NaCl, KCl); can state that compounds form by chemical combination of elements in fixed ratio; can write the formula of five common compounds (H2O, CO2, NaCl, HCl, NaOH).

title: Matter - states and interconversion revisited
subject: chem
definition:
Everything around us that has mass and occupies space is matter, and the same matter can appear in three different physical forms: solid, liquid and gas. In Class 6 you learnt that matter is made of tiny particles, and in Class 7 you met the kinetic theory, which says that these particles are always moving and that they attract one another. In this Class 8 revisit, the aim is to connect those ideas to the observable properties of each state and to the way one state can change into another.

A solid has a definite shape and a definite volume. If you hold an ice cube, a chalk stick or an iron nail, each keeps its own shape because its particles are packed very closely in a fixed, orderly arrangement. The intermolecular space between solid particles is the smallest of the three states, and the cohesive forces--the attractive forces between the particles--are strong enough to hold them in fixed positions. The particles can only vibrate about these fixed points; they do not move freely from place to place.

A liquid has a definite volume but no definite shape. A given volume of water, mercury or oil will take the shape of the glass, bottle or river bed that holds it. In a liquid, the particles are still quite close, so the cohesive forces remain strong, but they are no longer strong enough to keep the particles in fixed positions. The particles can slide past one another, which is why a liquid can flow and take the shape of its container. The intermolecular space is slightly larger than in a solid, giving the particles more freedom to move.

A gas has neither definite shape nor definite volume. Steam from a pressure cooker, the air in a balloon or the cooking gas in an LPG cylinder spreads out to fill the entire space available to it. Gas particles are far apart, the intermolecular space is very large, and the cohesive forces are almost negligible. The particles move rapidly and randomly in all directions, colliding with one another and with the walls of the container. This rapid, zig-zag, random motion of tiny suspended particles in a fluid is known as Brownian movement, and it provides visible evidence of the ceaseless motion of particles.

The three states are not permanent. Matter can change from one state to another through interconversion. When a solid is heated, its particles vibrate more vigorously. If they gain enough kinetic energy to overcome the strong cohesive forces, the solid melts into a liquid. Further heating makes the liquid particles move even faster, and when enough energy is supplied, they break away from one another completely and the liquid boils to form a gas. The reverse changes occur on cooling: a gas condenses to a liquid, and a liquid freezes to a solid. Some substances can change directly from solid to gas by sublimation, such as solid carbon dioxide or camphor, and the reverse is called deposition.

Heating and cooling also cause expansion and contraction. When matter is heated, the particles move more and take up more room, so the substance expands; on cooling, the particles slow down and the substance contracts. However, the particles themselves do not become larger or smaller; only their spacing and speed change. The particle model of matter therefore explains the states of matter, the interconversion between them, and the expansion and contraction we observe every day.
eli5: Everything you can touch, see or feel is made of tiny bits called particles. When these bits are packed tight and can only shake in place, you get a solid. When they can slide past each other but still stick close, you get a liquid. When they spread far apart and zoom around freely, you get a gas. Heating makes the bits move faster, which is how ice can turn to water and water can turn to steam.

diagnosticQuestions.question: Classify the three states of matter on the basis of shape and volume, and describe the arrangement of particles in each.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: A solid has a definite shape and a definite volume. Its particles are packed very closely in a fixed, orderly arrangement, with very little intermolecular space and strong cohesive forces. The particles can only vibrate about their fixed positions, which is why a solid cannot flow. A liquid has a definite volume but no definite shape; it takes the shape of the container it is placed in. The particles in a liquid are close together, so the cohesive forces are still strong, but the particles are not held in fixed positions. They can slide over one another, allowing the liquid to flow. A gas has neither definite shape nor definite volume; it expands to fill the entire container. The particles in a gas are far apart, the intermolecular space is very large, and the cohesive forces are almost negligible. The gas particles move rapidly and randomly in all directions, colliding with one another and with the walls of the container. Thus the differences in shape and volume can be explained by differences in the arrangement, spacing and motion of the particles.

diagnosticQuestions.question: Why does a gas fill the entire container while a solid keeps its own shape, even though the same substance is made of the same kind of particles in all three states?
diagnosticQuestions.answer: The same substance is made of the same type of particles in the solid, liquid and gas states, but the arrangement, spacing and motion of the particles are very different. In a solid, the particles are held very close together by strong cohesive forces in a fixed, regular pattern. Because the forces are strong and the particles are packed tightly, the solid has a fixed shape and volume. In a gas, the particles have gained much more kinetic energy, usually by heating, and the cohesive forces between them are almost negligible. The particles are therefore far apart and move rapidly in all directions. Since the particles are not held together, the gas spreads out and fills the entire space available to it. In other words, the shape and volume of a substance depend not on what the particles are, but on how much the particles are moving and how strongly they are attracted to one another. This is why the same water can be a rigid ice cube, a flowing liquid, or an expanding vapour depending on the conditions.

diagnosticQuestions.question: A student says, "When a solid is heated, the particles get bigger, so the solid expands. When it cools, the particles shrink, so the solid contracts." Evaluate this statement.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: This statement is not correct. The particles of a solid do not change in size when the solid is heated or cooled. A metal atom, a water molecule or an oxygen molecule remains the same size whether it is hot or cold. What changes is the amount of energy the particles have and therefore how much they move. When a solid is heated, the particles vibrate more vigorously about their fixed positions. Because they are moving more, they need a little more room, and the average distance between them increases. The whole object therefore expands. When the solid cools, the particles vibrate less and the average distance between them decreases, so the object contracts. The important point is that the particles themselves do not get bigger or smaller; the spaces between them change. There is also one important exception to the simple expansion-on-heating rule: water behaves unusually between about 4  deg C and 0  deg C. As water cools from 4  deg C to 0  deg C, it actually expands and becomes less dense, which is why ice floats on water. So the student's claim is partly based on a true observation--solids usually do expand on heating--but the explanation is completely wrong because it confuses the size of the particles with the space between them.

diagnosticQuestions.question: A metal ball passes through a metal ring when both are at room temperature. After the ball is heated strongly, it no longer passes through the ring. Explain this using the particle model of matter.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: When the metal ball is heated, it expands and its diameter increases. According to the particle model, the ball is made of metal atoms that are held close together in a regular arrangement. Heating gives these atoms more kinetic energy, so they vibrate more strongly about their fixed positions. Because the atoms are vibrating more, they take up slightly more space on average, and the average distance between them increases. This makes the whole metal ball expand outward in all directions, so its diameter becomes larger than the hole in the ring. The ring itself may also expand slightly, but if the ball is heated more than the ring, the ball's increase in size is greater and it cannot pass through. This is the same reason why railway tracks and metal bridges are laid with small gaps, and why a tight metal lid on a glass jar can sometimes be loosened by heating it. The particles do not themselves grow; the extra space between them makes the object bigger as a whole.

diagnosticQuestions.question: Design a simple classroom demonstration to show that there are spaces between the particles of a liquid and that the state of a substance can be changed by heating and cooling.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: One good demonstration uses water, alcohol, a measuring cylinder and a thermometer. First measure exactly 50 mL of water in a 100 mL measuring cylinder. Then measure exactly 50 mL of alcohol. Pour the alcohol slowly into the water. If the students watch carefully, the total volume of the mixture will be slightly less than 100 mL. This happens because the water particles and the alcohol particles are both made of molecules that have spaces between them, and some of the smaller molecules fit into the spaces between the larger molecules. This shows that matter is not continuous, but is made of tiny particles with intermolecular space between them. For the interconversion part, take a few ice cubes in a beaker and show that they melt into water when gently heated. Then heat the water in a flask with a one-holed stopper and a delivery tube, and show that steam is produced. When the steam hits a cold surface, such as a watch glass held above the delivery tube with ice in it, the steam condenses back into water droplets. This demonstration directly shows solid to liquid to gas and back to liquid by heating and cooling, and it gives students an opportunity to discuss how the particles move more on heating and less on cooling.

masteryCriteria: Can describe the three states of matter and their interconversion (melting, freezing, evaporation, condensation, sublimation); can explain interconversion in terms of particle arrangement and energy; can give one example of each interconversion process.

title: Chemical reactions - types revisited
subject: chem
definition:
A chemical reaction is a process in which one set of substances, called reactants, is converted into a different set of substances, called products. In this process the atoms are simply rearranged; none are created or destroyed, which is why a balanced chemical equation must have the same number of atoms of every element on both sides. In Class 8 we revisit the four major ways in which this rearrangement can occur, and we learn to show each change as a balanced chemical equation.

In a combination reaction, also called a synthesis reaction, two or more reactants join together to form a single product. The general pattern is A + B -> AB. A familiar example is the burning of magnesium in air: magnesium combines with oxygen to form magnesium oxide, 2Mg + O_2 -> 2MgO. Notice that two reactants become one product and the equation is balanced by placing a 2 in front of Mg and MgO.

In a decomposition reaction, sometimes called a breakdown reaction, a single compound splits into two or more simpler substances. The pattern is AB -> A + B. An example from everyday India is the heating of limestone, mainly calcium carbonate, in a lime kiln: CaCO_3 -> CaO + CO_2. The compound CaCO_3 breaks into calcium oxide and carbon dioxide. This is the opposite of combination.

In a displacement reaction, a more reactive element takes the place of a less reactive element in a compound. The pattern is A + BC -> AC + B. For instance, when a piece of zinc is dropped into dilute sulphuric acid, zinc displaces hydrogen: Zn + H_2SO_4 -> ZnSO_4 + H_2. Zinc is more reactive than hydrogen, so it pushes hydrogen out of the acid.

In a double displacement reaction, two compounds exchange partners. The pattern is AB + CD -> AD + CB. A classic example in the school laboratory is the reaction between silver nitrate solution and sodium chloride solution: AgNO_3 + NaCl -> AgCl + NaNO_3. The silver and sodium swap places, forming a white precipitate of silver chloride and sodium nitrate in solution.

To classify a reaction, first identify the reactants and products, then look at the way atoms are rearranged. If two or more substances become one, it is combination. If one substance breaks into several, it is decomposition. If one element replaces another in a compound, it is displacement. If two compounds swap ions to form two new compounds, it is double displacement. Whatever the type, every equation must be balanced, with correct chemical formulae and, where possible, the physical states written as symbols such as (s), (l), (g) or (aq). This skill is the language of chemistry.
eli5: Imagine building blocks. In a combination reaction, two small piles snap together into one big pile. In a decomposition, one big pile breaks into smaller piles. In a displacement, a stronger block kicks out a weaker block from a tower. In a double displacement, two towers swap some of their blocks to make two new towers. A balanced equation is just making sure you have the same number of blocks before and after.

misconceptions.belief: If I can see a single reactant on the left, the reaction must be decomposition, and if I can see a single compound breaking, the products must still be elements.
misconceptions.correction: Decomposition means one compound breaks into simpler substances, but the products can themselves be compounds. For example, CaCO_3 -> CaO + CO_2 gives two compounds, not elements. A compound can break into smaller compounds. The board examiner observations show that candidates often write wrong formulae for products, so always check the correct formula of every substance.

misconceptions.belief: I only need to write the correct names; the numbers in front do not matter much.
misconceptions.correction: The numbers, or coefficients, matter enormously because they balance the equation. Examiners regularly note that students do not balance equations. In the 2020 and Common board exam error pattern reports many candidates were penalised for unbalanced equations or for wrong formulae. For instance, writing Mg + O_2 -> MgO is wrong because there are two oxygen atoms on the left and only one on the right. The correct balanced form is 2Mg + O_2 -> 2MgO. Balancing is not optional; it is part of the correct answer.

misconceptions.belief: Displacement and double displacement are the same because both involve exchange.
misconceptions.correction: Displacement involves one element replacing another in a compound: A + BC -> AC + B. Double displacement involves two compounds exchanging ions with each other: AB + CD -> AD + CB. In displacement, a free element is always a reactant. In double displacement, both reactants are usually compounds. Watch for the presence of a free metal or non-metal on the left-hand side; that is your clue to displacement.

diagnosticQuestions.question: Define a chemical reaction. Give one example each of a combination reaction and a decomposition reaction, and write the balanced chemical equations for both.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: A chemical reaction is a process in which substances called reactants are changed into new substances called products, with the atoms being rearranged but not destroyed. In a combination reaction, two or more reactants combine to form a single product. For example, magnesium burns in oxygen to form magnesium oxide: 2Mg + O_2 -> 2MgO. This equation is balanced because there are two magnesium atoms and two oxygen atoms on each side. In a decomposition reaction, a single compound breaks down into two or more simpler substances. For example, calcium carbonate breaks down on heating to give calcium oxide and carbon dioxide: CaCO_3 -> CaO + CO_2. This equation is balanced because there is one calcium, one carbon and three oxygen atoms on each side. Both examples show how the same elements are present before and after the reaction; only the arrangement has changed. Combination is like joining two streams, and decomposition is like a tower of bricks falling apart.

diagnosticQuestions.question: A student says that burning a candle is only a physical change because the candle is still wax after the flame goes out. Explain, with reference to reactants and products, why the student is wrong.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: The student is wrong because burning is a chemical change, not a physical one. In a physical change, the substance remains the same and can usually be brought back to its original form, such as melting wax. In burning, the wax combines with oxygen from the air and changes completely into new substances such as carbon dioxide and water vapour. We can show this as a combination reaction in which the hydrocarbons in the wax react with oxygen to produce carbon dioxide and water. Once the wax has burned, you cannot recover the original wax simply by cooling the products. This is the key test of a chemical change: new products with new properties are formed and the change is difficult or impossible to reverse. The student is probably looking at the leftover solid wax near the wick, but the part that actually burned is gone, having been converted into gases that escape into the air. So burning a candle is a chemical reaction with new reactants and new products, just like cooking an egg, which cannot be uncooked.

diagnosticQuestions.question: A classmate states, "In every reaction that involves exchange, both reactants are compounds, so displacement and double displacement are actually the same type." Evaluate this statement, giving a balanced argument for and against before reaching a final judgement.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: The statement is not correct, but it does contain a small grain of truth that needs careful examination. On the one hand, both displacement and double displacement do involve rearrangement and exchange of atoms or ions. In double displacement, two compounds really do exchange ions with each other, as in AgNO_3 + NaCl -> AgCl + NaNO_3, where the silver and sodium ions swap places. Here both reactants are compounds, which matches part of the classmate's claim. On the other hand, the classmate's statement that both reactants are compounds in every exchange is clearly wrong for displacement. In a displacement reaction, one reactant is a free element, not a compound. For example, in Zn + H_2SO_4 -> ZnSO_4 + H_2, zinc is an element and sulphuric acid is a compound. The more reactive zinc displaces the less reactive hydrogen from the acid. Likewise, in Fe + CuSO_4 -> FeSO_4 + Cu, iron is an element that displaces copper from copper sulphate. Therefore the presence or absence of a free element is the key difference. The statement also confuses the general patterns: displacement follows A + BC -> AC + B, whereas double displacement follows AB + CD -> AD + CB. In the first case, only one partner changes; in the second case, both partners change. After weighing both sides, the final judgement is that the statement is incorrect. Displacement and double displacement are different reaction types, and the crucial clue is whether a free element is taking the place of another element in a compound, or whether two compounds are swapping ions.

diagnosticQuestions.question:
Four unbalanced or incomplete equations are given below. For each one, (i) classify the reaction as combination, decomposition, displacement or double displacement, (ii) complete the equation by writing the correct products, and (iii) balance the equation.
  (a) Zn + HCl ->
  (b) CaCO_3 -> CaO + CO_2
  (c) NaCl + AgNO_3 ->
  (d) H_2 + O_2 -> H_2O
diagnosticQuestions.answer: (a) This is a displacement reaction because zinc, a free element, displaces hydrogen from hydrochloric acid. The completed and balanced equation is Zn + 2HCl -> ZnCl_2 + H_2. We need 2HCl to give two hydrogen atoms on the left, matching the H_2 produced on the right. (b) This is a decomposition reaction because one compound breaks into two simpler compounds. The equation is already complete and balanced: CaCO_3 -> CaO + CO_2, with one calcium, one carbon and three oxygen atoms on each side. (c) This is a double displacement reaction because the two compounds exchange ions. The completed and balanced equation is NaCl + AgNO_3 -> AgCl + NaNO_3. A white precipitate of silver chloride forms, while sodium nitrate remains in solution. (d) This is a combination reaction because two elements combine to form one compound. The balanced equation is 2H_2 + O_2 -> 2H_2O. We need coefficients 2 in front of H_2 and H_2O so that there are four hydrogen atoms and two oxygen atoms on both sides.

diagnosticQuestions.question: Design a simple classroom activity using only common materials that would help a younger student understand the difference between combination and displacement reactions. Describe the materials, the procedure, and the observations that would let the student recognise each type.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: The activity needs two simple demonstrations. For the combination reaction, take a small piece of clean magnesium ribbon and a spirit lamp or Bunsen burner. Hold the magnesium with tongs and ignite it in air. The observation is a dazzling white flame and the formation of a white ash, magnesium oxide. Ask the younger student to notice that two things, the magnesium and the oxygen in the air, have joined to make one white powder. The activity drives home the idea A + B -> AB. For the displacement reaction, take a clean iron nail and a test tube filled with a little blue copper sulphate solution. Drop the nail into the solution and leave it for ten to fifteen minutes. The student will see the solution losing its blue colour and turning pale green, while a reddish-brown solid forms on the iron nail. Explain that the more reactive iron has pushed the less reactive copper out of the copper sulphate, just like a stronger player taking a weaker player's place in a team. The pattern is Fe + CuSO_4 -> FeSO_4 + Cu. After both demonstrations, ask the student to compare the two: in the first, two substances became one; in the second, a free metal replaced another metal in a compound. This contrast makes the classification clear and memorable.

masteryCriteria: Can name and define four types of chemical reactions (combination: A + B -> AB; decomposition: AB -> A + B; displacement: A + BC -> AC + B; double displacement: AB + CD -> AD + CB); can classify ten reactions correctly; can give one balanced equation for each type.

title: Combination reactions
subject: chem
definition: A combination reaction is a chemical change in which two or more reactants join together to produce a single product. The simplest way to remember this is the general form A + B -> AB: the substances on the left, the reactants, unite to form one new substance on the right, the product. This is why combination reactions are sometimes called synthesis reactions -- the word synthesis means putting things together to make something new. In every combination reaction, the product is a compound formed in a fixed proportion by the combining elements or compounds. For example, when carbon burns in oxygen, the two reactants combine to give only one product, carbon dioxide: C + O_2 -> CO_2. Notice that one element (carbon) joins with another element (oxygen) to give a single compound. A similar idea applies when iron and sulphur are heated together. Grey iron filings and yellow powdered sulphur, when strongly heated in a test tube or on a block, react to form a dark, brittle solid called iron sulphide: Fe + S -> FeS. This is a classic experiment used in Indian school laboratories to demonstrate combination because the product is clearly a single new substance with different properties from either starting material. Another important example is the formation of water: hydrogen and oxygen gases combine in a fixed ratio to give water, H_2O, as the only product. The burning of a candle is also a familiar combination process, because the wax (a hydrocarbon) combines with oxygen from the air to produce carbon dioxide and water vapour, although the visible flame reminds us that burning is a chemical change that releases energy. Combination reactions must be distinguished from other types of reactions. In a decomposition reaction, one compound breaks down into two or more simpler substances -- the opposite of combination. In a displacement reaction, one element replaces another in a compound, so there are two products or at least a rearrangement of atoms. In a double displacement reaction, two compounds exchange ions and usually form two new compounds or a precipitate. A combination reaction, by contrast, always has two or more reactants and exactly one product. When you write the balanced equation for a combination reaction, you must make sure that the number of atoms of each element is the same on both sides. The product will contain all the atoms of the reactants joined in a fixed proportion, so the balancing process is usually straightforward, but it still requires care. The key vocabulary to keep in mind is: combination reaction, reactant, product, single product, synthesis, chemical change, burning, compound formation, fixed proportion, oxygen, iron sulphide, candle, and joining. In the ICSE Class 8 syllabus, this node sits within the Language of Chemistry, and the expectation is that a student can define a combination reaction, identify one from a given chemical equation, and write balanced equations for common examples.
eli5: A combination reaction is like two or more things coming together to make one new thing. If you mix iron and sulphur and heat them, they become a single solid called iron sulphide. If carbon burns in air, it joins with oxygen to make one gas called carbon dioxide. In every combination reaction, several reactants join to give a single product.

misconceptions.belief: Students often write oxygen as a single atom "O" instead of the molecule "O_2". board examiners have noted that many candidates lose marks because they do not use the correct form of an element in equations.
misconceptions.correction: Oxygen is a diatomic gas; always write O_2 in equations unless it appears as an ion in a compound. When carbon burns, the correct equation is C + O_2 -> CO_2, not C + O -> CO.

misconceptions.belief: Some students think that iron sulphide is just a mixture of iron and sulphur. This is wrong because a mixture keeps the properties of its parts and can often be separated physically, but the product of heating iron and sulphur is a new compound with fixed proportion and different properties. The examiner observations mention that candidates sometimes get the formula or product wrong in reactions.
misconceptions.correction: Fe + S -> FeS is a compound formation, not a mixture. The iron and sulphur atoms have combined chemically in a fixed proportion.

misconceptions.belief: Students sometimes treat any reaction with burning as a combination reaction, even if several products form. The board exam guidance show that pupils often write incomplete or unbalanced equations when products are missed.
misconceptions.correction: A true combination reaction has two or more reactants forming a single product. Burning a candle in air produces carbon dioxide and water, so it is not a single-product combination reaction in the strict sense, although the act of burning involves combination with oxygen.

diagnosticQuestions.question: Define a combination reaction and give one example from the syllabus with a balanced equation.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: A combination reaction is a chemical change in which two or more reactants join together to form a single product. The general form of a combination reaction is A + B -> AB, where A and B are the reactants and AB is the new compound produced. One important example from the syllabus is the burning of carbon in oxygen. Carbon is an element that exists as a black solid, such as charcoal or graphite, and oxygen is a colourless diatomic gas present in the air. When carbon is heated in a plentiful supply of oxygen, the two reactants combine to form a single product, carbon dioxide, which is a colourless gas. The balanced chemical equation for this reaction is C + O_2 -> CO_2. This equation is balanced because there is one carbon atom and two oxygen atoms on the left-hand side and one carbon atom and two oxygen atoms on the right-hand side. Another example from the syllabus is the heating of iron with sulphur to form iron sulphide, Fe + S -> FeS. In both cases, the key feature is that more than one reactant gives exactly one product, and the reaction is a true chemical change because the product has new properties that are different from the reactants.

diagnosticQuestions.question: Why is the reaction between iron and sulphur on heating called a combination reaction? Explain with reference to the number of reactants and products, and state how you would show that the grey product is a compound and not a mixture.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: The reaction between iron and sulphur on heating is called a combination reaction because it fits the pattern A + B -> AB. The two starting substances, iron and sulphur, are the reactants, and they combine to form one single product, iron sulphide. The reactants are an element, iron, and another element, sulphur, and the product is a compound. The equation is Fe + S -> FeS. To show that the product is a compound and not a mixture, you can carry out a simple test. Before heating, you can separate the iron filings from the sulphur powder using a magnet because iron is magnetic but sulphur is not. After heating, the product iron sulphide is no longer magnetic, so a magnet will not pull out any iron. Also, a mixture of iron and sulphur would keep the yellow colour of sulphur and the grey colour of iron, but iron sulphide is a dark grey or black brittle solid with a colour and texture of its own. A compound is formed in a fixed proportion, while a mixture can be mixed in any proportion. In the FeS compound, iron and sulphur are always present in a fixed mass ratio, which is one reason the chemical formula is FeS. Because the product is a single new compound with different properties, the reaction is correctly classified as a combination reaction.

diagnosticQuestions.question: A student writes the equation for the formation of magnesium oxide as Mg + O -> MgO. Evaluate this equation and explain whether it is a good representation of the combination reaction between magnesium and oxygen.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: The student's equation Mg + O -> MgO is not a good representation of the combination reaction between magnesium and oxygen, although the product formula MgO is correct. There are two main problems. First, oxygen exists as a diatomic molecule in its natural state, so the correct reactant is O_2 and not O. Second, the equation as written is not balanced if O is replaced by O_2. The correct balanced equation is 2Mg + O_2 -> 2MgO. This equation has two magnesium atoms and two oxygen atoms on the left, and two magnesium atoms and two oxygen atoms on the right, so it is balanced. It also correctly shows that two reactants, magnesium metal and oxygen gas, combine to form one product, magnesium oxide. The original equation Mg + O -> MgO gives the wrong form of oxygen and could mislead someone into thinking that oxygen exists as single atoms when it does not. In the ICSE board exam, equations with O instead of O_2 and equations that are not balanced are common reasons for losing marks, as the examiner observations have shown. Therefore, the student should be praised for knowing the product formula, but corrected for the reactant form and for not balancing the equation. A good answer must show O_2 and balance the atoms. If the student understands that oxygen is diatomic and that coefficients can be used to balance, the equation can be made correct and complete.

diagnosticQuestions.question: Write balanced chemical equations for the following combination reactions and identify the reactants and the single product in each case. (a) Carbon burns in oxygen to form carbon dioxide. (b) Hydrogen and oxygen combine to form water. (c) Iron and sulphur are heated to form iron sulphide. (d) Calcium oxide reacts with water to form calcium hydroxide.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: (a) Carbon burns in oxygen to form carbon dioxide. The reactants are carbon, C, and oxygen, O_2. The single product is carbon dioxide, CO_2. The balanced equation is C + O_2 -> CO_2. The atoms are balanced because there is one carbon and two oxygen atoms on each side. (b) Hydrogen and oxygen combine to form water. The reactants are hydrogen, H_2, and oxygen, O_2. The single product is water, H_2O. To balance the equation, we need two hydrogen molecules and one oxygen molecule to give two water molecules: 2H_2 + O_2 -> 2H_2O. Now there are four hydrogen atoms and two oxygen atoms on the left, and four hydrogen atoms and two oxygen atoms on the right. (c) Iron and sulphur are heated to form iron sulphide. The reactants are iron, Fe, and sulphur, S. The single product is iron sulphide, FeS. The balanced equation is Fe + S -> FeS, which is already balanced with one iron atom and one sulphur atom on each side. The reaction is usually shown with a triangle or the word "heat" over the arrow, Fe + S -> FeS, because heat is required. (d) Calcium oxide reacts with water to form calcium hydroxide. The reactants are calcium oxide, CaO, and water, H_2O. The single product is calcium hydroxide, Ca(OH)_2. The balanced equation is CaO + H_2O -> Ca(OH)_2. This is also a combination reaction because two reactants give one product. In all four cases, the defining feature is that more than one reactant joins to form a single product, and the equations are balanced.

diagnosticQuestions.question: Imagine you are asked to design a small classroom demonstration to help your classmates understand that a combination reaction produces a single new product with different properties from the reactants. Describe the materials, the procedure, the expected observation, and how you would explain the result using a balanced equation.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: For the classroom demonstration, I would use the reaction between iron filings and sulphur powder to form iron sulphide. The materials needed are fine iron filings, powdered sulphur, a glass test tube or a porcelain dish, a Bunsen burner or spirit lamp, a pair of tongs, and a small magnet. First, I would mix the iron filings and sulphur powder in the correct proportions on a piece of paper. Then I would pour the mixture into the test tube and heat it gently at first and then strongly using the Bunsen burner. I would expect to see the sulphur melting and then the mixture glowing red as the reaction starts. After heating for a few minutes, a dark grey or black brittle solid would form at the bottom of the tube. Once the tube has cooled, I would pass a magnet over the product. I would observe that the product is not attracted to the magnet, which shows that the iron has combined chemically and is no longer present as free iron. I would also point out that the yellow colour of sulphur has disappeared and a new substance with a different colour and texture has been formed. I would explain the result with the balanced equation Fe + S -> FeS. This equation shows that one atom of iron combines with one atom of sulphur to give one formula unit of iron sulphide. Because the product is a single new compound with fixed composition and different properties, this is a good example of a combination reaction. As an extra check, I might compare this product with a simple mixture of iron and sulphur that has not been heated; the mixture would still be attracted to a magnet and would show both colours, which makes the difference between a mixture and a compound clear.

masteryCriteria: Can define combination reactions (two or more reactants form one product); can write three balanced equations (C + O2 -> CO2; 2H2 + O2 -> 2H2O; CaO + H2O -> Ca(OH)2); can identify combination reactions from given examples.

title: Decomposition reactions
subject: chem
definition:
A decomposition reaction is a chemical change in which one compound, made of two or more elements chemically combined in fixed and definite proportions, breaks down into two or more simpler substances. In any compound, the original properties of the constituent elements are lost and a new substance with its own characteristic properties is formed; a decomposition reaction reverses that kind of union by splitting the compound into simpler products. The key signature of a decomposition reaction is that there is a single reactant on the left-hand side of the chemical equation and two or more products on the right-hand side. This is why it is often described as the opposite of a combination reaction: where combination joins substances, decomposition tears them apart.

Decomposition reactions are classified according to the kind of energy that drives the breakdown. Thermal decomposition takes place when heat is supplied; the compound absorbs heat and then splits. A classic example is calcium carbonate, found as limestone or marble in many parts of India, which on strong heating in a lime kiln decomposes into calcium oxide, called quicklime, and carbon dioxide gas. Electrolytic decomposition, also called electrolysis, occurs when an electric current is passed through a compound, usually in the molten state or in aqueous solution, causing it to break into its constituent elements. The electrolysis of water is the best-known example, giving hydrogen and oxygen gases. Photolytic decomposition occurs when light, especially sunlight, supplies the energy needed; silver chloride turns grey or black in sunlight because it decomposes into silver and chlorine. It is important to write these changes as balanced chemical equations and to show the condition -- heat, electricity or light -- above or below the arrow. A balanced equation obeys the law of conservation of mass and tells us exactly how many formula units of reactant produce the products. The equations are:

CaCO3 -> CaO + CO2 (Heat)
2H2O -> 2H2 + O2 (Electricity)
2AgCl -> 2Ag + Cl2 (Sunlight)

Teachers also ask students to contrast decomposition with the burning of a candle. A candle appears to disappear, but the wax does not simply break down on its own; it combines with oxygen from the air in a combustion reaction, releasing carbon dioxide, water vapour and energy. Knowing how to recognise the single reactant and the energy source is the heart of answering questions on this topic.
eli5: Imagine you have a big Lego house. A decomposition reaction is like taking that house apart and getting back smaller bricks. Sometimes you need to pull the pieces apart with your hands, sometimes you use a tool, and sometimes strong sunlight does the work. In chemistry, one compound breaks into two or more simpler pieces when we add heat, electricity, or light.

diagnosticQuestions.question: Define a decomposition reaction and name its three types, giving one balanced equation for each type.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: A decomposition reaction is a chemical change in which a single compound breaks down into two or more simpler substances. The simplest way to remember it is the pattern AB -> A + B. The number 'one' on the left and 'more than one' on the right is the key. The three types are classified by the energy source that drives the breakdown. Thermal decomposition is caused by heat, such as calcium carbonate decomposing into calcium oxide and carbon dioxide on strong heating: CaCO3 -> CaO + CO2 (Heat). Electrolytic decomposition is caused by an electric current passed through a compound, such as water being split by electrolysis: 2H2O -> 2H2 + O2 (Electricity). Photolytic decomposition is caused by light, such as silver chloride turning grey in sunlight: 2AgCl -> 2Ag + Cl2 (Sunlight). Each equation has one reactant on the left and two products on the right, and each carries the condition above the arrow.

diagnosticQuestions.question: Hydrogen peroxide decomposes in the presence of sunlight into water and oxygen. Is this thermal, photolytic or electrolytic decomposition? Explain using the meaning of the terms and a balanced equation.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: The decomposition of hydrogen peroxide in sunlight is a photolytic decomposition. The term 'photolytic' comes from 'photo' meaning light and 'lysis' meaning breaking; so the energy for the breakdown is supplied by light. It is not thermal because no heat is being supplied as the driving condition, and it is not electrolytic because no electric current is being passed through the liquid. The balanced equation is 2H2O2 --Sunlight--> 2H2O + O2. On the left there is only hydrogen peroxide, a single reactant, and on the right there are two products, water and oxygen, which is exactly the pattern of a decomposition reaction. Counting the atoms on both sides: four hydrogen atoms and four oxygen atoms on the left, and the same on the right, so the equation is balanced. In an Indian school laboratory, a dilute solution of hydrogen peroxide in a clear test tube will bubble gently when exposed to bright sunlight because oxygen gas is being released.

diagnosticQuestions.question: A classmate says, "The thermal decomposition of calcium carbonate is the exact reverse of the combination reaction between calcium and oxygen; therefore, the products of the decomposition are calcium and oxygen gas." Evaluate this claim with a balanced, supported argument.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: The classmate's statement is incorrect, and the reasoning contains two serious mistakes. First, not every decomposition reaction is the simple reverse of a direct combination of the elements in the compound. Calcium carbonate, for example, is not made by directly combining calcium metal and oxygen gas; it is made from calcium oxide and carbon dioxide. Therefore, the thermal decomposition of calcium carbonate is better understood as the reverse of the reaction between calcium oxide and carbon dioxide, not the combination of calcium and oxygen. Second, the products of the decomposition are not calcium and oxygen gas. Strong heating of calcium carbonate gives calcium oxide and carbon dioxide: CaCO3 -> CaO + CO2 (Heat). If the products really were calcium and oxygen, the residue would be a shiny, reactive metal, but the actual residue is a white powder, quicklime, and the gas is carbon dioxide, which turns limewater milky. The student's error shows the danger of guessing products from the name of the elements in the compound rather than from experimental observation and a correctly balanced equation. A balanced, supported answer would mention the white residue, the limewater test, and the condition written above the arrow. Therefore, the claim is false and the correct decomposition products are calcium oxide and carbon dioxide.

diagnosticQuestions.question: A white powder was strongly heated in a hard glass test tube. A colourless gas was evolved which turned limewater milky, and a white residue was left behind. Name the likely white powder, the type of decomposition, the products and write a balanced equation. Suggest one safety precaution and one confirming test.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: The white powder is most likely calcium carbonate, which occurs naturally as limestone or marble. The colourless gas that turns limewater milky is carbon dioxide, a classic test for CO2. The reaction is a thermal decomposition because it is brought about by strong heating. The balanced equation is CaCO3(s) -> CaO(s) + CO2(g), with the word 'Heat' written above the arrow. The white residue left in the test tube is calcium oxide, also called quicklime. Before performing the experiment, one safety precaution is to heat the test tube slightly tilted and pointed away from the face, and to wear safety goggles, because the sudden release of hot gas can crack the glass. To confirm the gas, bubble it through freshly prepared limewater; the solution turns milky, proving the gas is carbon dioxide. The residue can be tested with a drop of water: if it is calcium oxide, it will hiss and form calcium hydroxide, releasing enough heat to be felt.

diagnosticQuestions.question: Design a simple classroom activity to demonstrate the electrolytic decomposition of water. List the materials, the steps, the expected observations and how you would show that the gases are hydrogen and oxygen. Explain the symbol you would write above the arrow in the balanced equation.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: Materials: two carbon electrodes, a 6-volt battery or cell, connecting wires, a small beaker, acidulated water, two small test tubes filled with water and inverted over the electrodes, and a wooden splint. Steps: set up the apparatus so that the two electrodes are dipped in acidulated water and the test tubes are placed over them to collect the gases. Switch on the current. Observation: bubbles form immediately at both electrodes. The gas collected at the cathode is hydrogen, and the gas at the anode is oxygen; the volume of hydrogen is about twice that of oxygen. Test the gases by bringing a burning splint near each tube: hydrogen burns with a 'pop', while oxygen relights a glowing splint. The equation is 2H2O(l) --Electricity--> 2H2(g) + O2(g). The symbol or word written above the arrow should be 'Electricity' or 'Electrolysis', not H2SO4 or any other substance. This demonstration proves that water, a single compound, has broken down into two simpler substances, hydrogen and oxygen, using electrical energy, which is the defining feature of electrolytic decomposition.

masteryCriteria: Can define decomposition reactions (one reactant breaks into two or more products); can write three balanced equations (2HgO -> 2Hg + O2; CaCO3 -> CaO + CO2; 2H2O -> 2H2 + O2); can classify decomposition as thermal, photo, or electrolytic.

title: Displacement reactions
subject: chem
definition: A displacement reaction is a chemical reaction in which a more reactive element removes, or displaces, a less reactive element from a compound. The general pattern is A + BC -> AC + B, where A is the more reactive element, BC is the compound, and B is the less reactive element that is driven out. Because only one element is being replaced by another, this type of reaction is also called a single replacement or single displacement reaction. Whether one metal can displace another from a compound is decided by the reactivity series of metals. A metal higher up in the reactivity series can displace a metal lower down from its salt solution. For example, zinc is more reactive than copper, so when zinc pieces or granules are added to a blue copper sulphate solution, zinc displaces copper from copper sulphate and forms colourless zinc sulphate, while brown copper metal settles out. The equation is Zn + CuSO_4 -> ZnSO_4 + Cu. Similarly, iron being more reactive than copper can displace copper from copper sulphate, giving greenish iron(II) sulphate and copper: Fe + CuSO_4 -> FeSO_4 + Cu. Metals such as magnesium and zinc can also displace hydrogen from dilute hydrochloric acid. Magnesium, being high in the reactivity series, can even displace hydrogen from steam, forming magnesium oxide and hydrogen gas. To identify a displacement reaction from a given equation, look for one element reacting with a compound and producing a different compound plus a free element. To write balanced equations for displacement reactions, first write the correct formulae of the reactants and products, then adjust coefficients so that the number of atoms of each element is the same on both sides. Displacement reactions must not be confused with combination reactions, in which two or more substances combine to form a single product such as 2Mg + O_2 -> 2MgO, or with decomposition reactions, in which a single compound breaks into two or more simpler substances such as CaCO_3 -> CaO + CO_2. In a displacement reaction, the total number of compounds and elements is not reduced to one, nor is one compound simply split apart; rather, one element takes the place of another inside a compound, giving a new compound and a free element.
eli5: In a displacement reaction, a stronger metal kicks out a weaker metal from its compound. It is like a stronger player joining a team and replacing a weaker player. The stronger metal takes the place, and the weaker one is pushed out.

diagnosticQuestions.question: Define a displacement reaction and write two balanced equations to illustrate it, one involving a metal displacing another metal from a salt solution and one involving a metal displacing hydrogen from an acid.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: A displacement reaction is a reaction in which a more reactive element removes a less reactive element from a compound. The general pattern is A + BC -> AC + B, where A is the more reactive element. This is also called a single replacement reaction. One well-known example is the reaction between zinc and copper sulphate. Zinc is above copper in the reactivity series, so zinc can displace copper. The balanced equation is Zn + CuSO_4 -> ZnSO_4 + Cu. We observe that the blue colour of the copper sulphate solution fades and a reddish brown coating of copper forms on the zinc. Another example is the reaction between zinc and dilute hydrochloric acid. Zinc is more reactive than hydrogen, so it displaces hydrogen from the acid. The balanced equation is Zn + 2HCl -> ZnCl_2 + H_2. Bubbles of hydrogen gas are given off and the zinc granules dissolve to form zinc chloride solution.

diagnosticQuestions.question: Explain why a piece of iron can displace copper from copper sulphate solution, but a piece of copper cannot displace iron from iron(II) sulphate solution. Refer to the reactivity series in your answer.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: Whether one metal displaces another from a compound depends on the relative positions of the two metals in the reactivity series. A metal that is higher in the series is more reactive and can displace a metal lower in the series from its salt solution. Iron is placed above copper in the reactivity series. Therefore, when iron is added to copper sulphate solution, the more reactive iron replaces the less reactive copper. The iron atoms lose electrons to become iron(II) ions and go into solution, while copper(II) ions gain electrons and come out as copper metal. The equation is Fe + CuSO_4 -> FeSO_4 + Cu. On the other hand, copper is below iron in the reactivity series. Copper is less reactive than iron, so it does not have enough tendency to remove iron from iron(II) sulphate. If a piece of copper is placed in iron(II) sulphate solution, no visible reaction occurs. The copper does not displace the iron, and the greenish colour of the solution remains unchanged. This comparison shows that reactivity is not a matter of choice; it is fixed by the position of each metal in the reactivity series.

diagnosticQuestions.question: A student states: 'The reaction between magnesium and hydrochloric acid, Mg + 2HCl -> MgCl_2 + H_2, is a double displacement reaction because two different pairs of atoms exchange places.' Evaluate this statement with a balanced argument.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: The student's statement is not correct. The reaction Mg + 2HCl -> MgCl_2 + H_2 is a displacement reaction, not a double displacement reaction. In a double displacement reaction, two compounds exchange ions to form two new compounds, and no free element is produced. The general pattern is AB + CD -> AD + CB. The given reaction, however, starts with an element, magnesium, and a compound, hydrochloric acid. It ends with a new compound, magnesium chloride, and a free element, hydrogen gas. The pattern matches A + BC -> AC + B, which is the signature of a single displacement reaction. The student is partly right that atoms are rearranged, but the label of 'double displacement' is wrong because the reactants are not two compounds and because a free element is produced. It is important to name reactions by the number of elements and compounds on each side. The correct name is a single displacement or displacement reaction. Therefore, the student's claim should be rejected and the reaction should be classified as displacement of hydrogen from the acid by the more reactive metal magnesium.

diagnosticQuestions.question: A test tube contains a blue solution of copper(II) sulphate. A small piece of zinc is dropped into one half of the solution and a small piece of silver is dropped into the other half. Predict what you would observe in each case and write balanced equations where a reaction occurs. Explain your predictions using the reactivity series.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: In the first case, when a piece of zinc is placed in copper sulphate solution, a reaction takes place because zinc is more reactive than copper and lies above copper in the reactivity series. Zinc displaces copper from copper sulphate. We would observe that the blue colour of the solution slowly fades as copper ions are removed, and a reddish brown solid of copper metal appears on the zinc strip or at the bottom of the tube. The balanced equation is Zn + CuSO_4 -> ZnSO_4 + Cu. In the second case, when a piece of silver is placed in copper sulphate solution, no reaction occurs. Silver is below copper in the reactivity series, so it is less reactive and cannot displace copper from copper sulphate. The solution remains blue and the silver strip stays shiny. Therefore, the only reaction in this situation is the one involving zinc. This practical test confirms that reactivity series predictions match what we see in the laboratory.

diagnosticQuestions.question: Design a simple school-laboratory activity that demonstrates a displacement reaction between a metal and a salt solution. List the materials, the procedure, the expected observation, the safety precautions, and the conclusion.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: Aim: To demonstrate that a more reactive metal displaces a less reactive metal from its salt solution. Materials required: a clean test tube, dilute copper sulphate solution, a small strip of zinc metal or a few zinc granules, a glass rod or spatula, and a Bunsen burner or hot water bath to warm the solution gently if needed. Procedure: Pour about 5 ml of copper sulphate solution into the test tube. Note its blue colour. Add a piece of zinc or a few zinc granules. Leave the tube for a few minutes, stirring occasionally. Observe any colour change or deposit on the metal. Expected observation: The blue colour of the copper sulphate solution becomes lighter and finally almost colourless. A reddish brown solid, copper, is deposited on the zinc or settles at the bottom. If the reaction is slow, gentle warming can speed it up. Safety precautions: Wear safety goggles and an apron. Handle dilute copper sulphate with care because it can stain skin and clothes. Do not touch the zinc granules with bare hands if the acid is used. Dispose of the metal and solution according to school safety rules. Conclusion: Zinc is more reactive than copper, so it displaces copper from copper sulphate. The reaction is a displacement reaction, and the equation Zn + CuSO_4 -> ZnSO_4 + Cu explains the observations.

masteryCriteria: Can define displacement reactions (more reactive element displaces less reactive from compound); can write three balanced equations (Fe + CuSO4 -> FeSO4 + Cu; Zn + 2HCl -> ZnCl2 + H2; Cl2 + 2KI -> 2KCl + I2); can use the reactivity series to predict if a reaction occurs.

title: Double displacement reactions
subject: chem
definition:
A double displacement reaction is a chemical change in which the positive and negative ions of two ionic compounds exchange places, so that each cation ends up paired with the other anion, producing two entirely new compounds. The general pattern can be written as AB + CD -> AD + CB, where A and C are the positive ions, while B and D are the negative ions. This type of change is also called an ion exchange reaction because the ions of the two reactants literally swap partners. In Class 8 you are expected to recognise this pattern, to identify a double displacement reaction when you see an equation, and to write balanced equations for two important sub-types: precipitation reactions and neutralisation reactions.

In a precipitation reaction, one of the new compounds formed is insoluble in water and appears as a solid, called the precipitate. The classic school-laboratory example is silver nitrate reacting with sodium chloride. Silver nitrate solution, AgNO3, is colourless; sodium chloride solution, NaCl, is also colourless. When they are mixed, the silver ion (Ag+) from silver nitrate swaps with the sodium ion (Na+) from sodium chloride. The products are sodium nitrate (NaNO3), which stays dissolved, and silver chloride (AgCl), which is so insoluble that it immediately forms a white precipitate. The equation is AgNO3(aq) + NaCl(aq) -> NaNO3(aq) + AgCl(s)v. Another common example is barium chloride reacting with sodium sulphate. The barium ion (Ba2+) from barium chloride exchanges with the sodium ion (Na+) from sodium sulphate, giving sodium chloride in solution and barium sulphate as a white precipitate: BaCl2(aq) + Na2SO4(aq) -> 2NaCl(aq) + BaSO4(s)v. The downward arrow next to the formula is the standard way of showing that a solid precipitate has formed.

In a neutralisation reaction, an acid reacts with a base or an alkali and the ion exchange produces a salt and water. A well-known example is sodium hydroxide reacting with hydrochloric acid. The sodium ion (Na+) from sodium hydroxide swaps with the hydrogen ion (H+) from hydrochloric acid, while the hydroxide ion (OH-) from the base swaps with the chloride ion (Cl-) from the acid. The new pairings are sodium chloride (NaCl) and water (H2O): NaOH(aq) + HCl(aq) -> NaCl(aq) + H2O(l). Notice that in neutralisation there is no precipitate; instead, heat is released and the resulting solution contains a salt. Because the reaction involves two reactants and two products, it is still a double displacement reaction, even though the visible change is different from the milky precipitate seen with silver nitrate and sodium chloride.

The reason a precipitate forms is that one of the new combinations of ions is insoluble in water, so the ions cannot remain freely moving in solution and join together as tiny solid particles. This is like clouds condensing into raindrops: the dissolved ions, invisible in solution, suddenly come together to make a visible solid. A useful way to remember double displacement is to think of two couples at a dance swapping partners: the positive and negative ions rearrange themselves. When you write the balanced equation, you must make sure that the same number of each type of atom appears on both sides and that the formulas of the products are correct after the exchange.
eli5: Imagine two pairs of dance partners. In a double displacement reaction, the partners swap: person A leaves B to dance with D, while C leaves D to dance with B. In chemicals, two compounds swap their ions and make two new compounds. Sometimes the new product is an insoluble solid called a precipitate, like white clouds forming in the test tube.

misconceptions.belief: Students confuse the observation with the product. board exam guidance from the 2025 and 2020 Common board exam error pattern note that several candidates "wrote the reactions or named the product instead of writing the observations." In a precipitation reaction the expected observation is the formation of a white precipitate.
misconceptions.correction: the observation describes what you see, such as "a white precipitate is formed"; the product is the substance, such as "silver chloride." Both are needed, but they are not the same thing.

misconceptions.belief: Students fail to balance the equation after exchanging ions. Examiners have observed that candidates can identify reactants but make errors in the products and in the condition keywords. In a double displacement equation such as BaCl2 + Na2SO4 -> 2NaCl + BaSO4, the "2" in front of NaCl is necessary because barium chloride supplies two chloride ions and sodium sulphate supplies two sodium ions.
misconceptions.correction: after writing the formulas by ion exchange, always count atoms on each side and add coefficients to balance the equation.

misconceptions.belief: Students think neutralisation is not a double displacement reaction because no precipitate appears. Since a precipitate is the most obvious sign of double displacement in the laboratory, some students assume that the absence of a solid means the reaction is not a double displacement.
misconceptions.correction: any reaction of the type AB + CD -> AD + CB is a double displacement. In neutralisation, the H+ and OH- combine to form water while the metal ion and the non-metal ion form a salt, so it is still an ion exchange reaction.

diagnosticQuestions.question: Define a double displacement reaction and write its general equation.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: A double displacement reaction is a reaction between two ionic compounds in which the positive and negative ions exchange partners, giving two new compounds. It is also called an ion exchange reaction. The general pattern is AB + CD -> AD + CB, where A and C are the positive ions and B and D are the negative ions. For example, when silver nitrate solution is mixed with sodium chloride solution, the Ag+ ion from silver nitrate pairs with the Cl- ion from sodium chloride to form insoluble silver chloride, while the Na+ ion pairs with the NO3- ion to form sodium nitrate. The formation of an insoluble solid from the reaction is called a precipitate, and the reaction is described as a precipitation reaction. If the reactants are an acid and a base, the reaction is called a neutralisation reaction. In all cases, double displacement is recognised by the swap of ions between the two reactants.

diagnosticQuestions.question: Explain why a white precipitate is formed when barium chloride solution is added to sodium sulphate solution. Name the precipitate and write the balanced equation.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: Barium chloride and sodium sulphate are both soluble ionic compounds in water. When their solutions are mixed, the barium ions (Ba2+) and the sodium ions (Na+) have the chance to swap partners. The barium ion combines with the sulphate ion (SO4 2-) to form barium sulphate, BaSO4, which is insoluble in water. Because it is insoluble, the barium and sulphate ions leave the solution as tiny solid particles, making the mixture look cloudy or white. This insoluble solid is the precipitate, and in this case it is a white precipitate of barium sulphate. The sodium ions combine with the chloride ions to form sodium chloride, which stays dissolved. Since one barium chloride unit contains one barium ion and two chloride ions, and one sodium sulphate unit contains two sodium ions and one sulphate ion, the equation must be balanced with two sodium chloride formula units: BaCl2(aq) + Na2SO4(aq) -> 2NaCl(aq) + BaSO4(s)v. The downward arrow shows the formation of the precipitate.

diagnosticQuestions.question: A student says, "A neutralisation reaction between sodium hydroxide and hydrochloric acid is not a double displacement reaction because no precipitate is formed." Is the student correct? Give reasons for and against the statement.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: The student is not correct, but the statement contains a partial truth that needs to be examined carefully. On the one side, it is true that many double displacement reactions are recognised by the formation of a precipitate, and neutralisation does not produce a solid. In the laboratory, sodium hydroxide and hydrochloric acid are both colourless solutions, and the resulting mixture is also colourless, so there is no visible precipitate. That can make it seem different from the silver nitrate and sodium chloride reaction, where a white precipitate appears immediately. However, the definition of a double displacement reaction is based on the exchange of ions between two reactants, not on the presence or absence of a precipitate. In the neutralisation of sodium hydroxide with hydrochloric acid, the sodium ion (Na+) from the sodium hydroxide pairs with the chloride ion (Cl-) from the acid, while the hydrogen ion (H+) from the acid pairs with the hydroxide ion (OH-) from the alkali. The new pairings are NaCl and H2O, so the reaction follows the pattern AB + CD -> AD + CB. Therefore, it is a double displacement reaction. A balanced equation is NaOH(aq) + HCl(aq) -> NaCl(aq) + H2O(l). The visible evidence of neutralisation is the release of heat and the formation of a salt solution, not a solid. So the student is right to notice the absence of a precipitate but wrong to conclude that the reaction is not a double displacement. The correct criterion is ion exchange.

diagnosticQuestions.question: You are given four unlabelled solutions: sodium hydroxide, hydrochloric acid, silver nitrate, and barium chloride. Describe a simple test to identify which two will give a double displacement reaction with a white precipitate, and write the balanced equation for any one such reaction.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: To identify a precipitation-type double displacement reaction, I would mix small samples of each pair of solutions and look for the formation of a white precipitate. For example, I would take a little silver nitrate solution and add it to sodium chloride solution if one is available, or mix silver nitrate with any solution that contains chloride ions. In the given list, hydrochloric acid contains chloride ions, so mixing silver nitrate with hydrochloric acid will produce a white precipitate of silver chloride. Another possible pair from the list is barium chloride with sodium sulphate, but sodium sulphate is not in the list, so the practical test within the given chemicals would be to mix silver nitrate with hydrochloric acid. When silver nitrate solution and hydrochloric acid are mixed, the Ag+ ion from silver nitrate exchanges with the H+ ion from the acid, forming silver chloride, which is insoluble, and nitric acid, which remains in solution. The white precipitate is silver chloride. The balanced equation is AgNO3(aq) + HCl(aq) -> AgCl(s)v + HNO3(aq). This shows a double displacement because the positive ions Ag+ and H+ have changed partners between the nitrate and chloride negative ions.

diagnosticQuestions.question: Design a short laboratory activity that would let a Class 8 student observe and record a double displacement reaction, including the materials needed, the expected observation, and one safety rule.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: The activity could be titled "Forming a white precipitate by double displacement." The materials needed are dilute silver nitrate solution, dilute sodium chloride solution, two clean test tubes, a test-tube holder, a dropper, white paper to view the colour change clearly, and a waste beaker for used chemicals. The student should first place about 2 cm3 of sodium chloride solution in a test tube. Then, using a dropper, add about 1 cm3 of silver nitrate solution. The student should record the immediate observation, which is the formation of a white precipitate that makes the solution look milky or cloudy. The white solid is silver chloride, and the product that stays in solution is sodium nitrate. The balanced equation to be written is AgNO3(aq) + NaCl(aq) -> AgCl(s)v + NaNO3(aq). One important safety rule is to wear safety goggles and avoid touching the solutions, because silver nitrate can stain the skin and the chemicals should not be ingested or allowed to contact the eyes. After the activity, the mixture should be poured into the waste beaker and the test tubes rinsed thoroughly.

masteryCriteria: Can define double displacement reactions (ions exchange between two compounds); can write three balanced equations (AgNO3 + NaCl -> AgCl + NaNO3; BaCl2 + Na2SO4 -> BaSO4 + 2NaCl; Pb(NO3)2 + 2KI -> PbI2 + 2KNO3); can identify the precipitate in each reaction.

title: Carbon and its compounds - bonding
subject: chem
definition:
