Carbon, with the atomic number 6, is the element that occupies a unique position in chemistry because of the way it bonds with itself and with other elements. Its electronic configuration is 2,4, which tells us that there are two electrons in its first shell and four electrons in its outermost, or valence, shell. According to the octet rule, an atom becomes stable when its outermost shell contains eight electrons. Because carbon has four electrons in the valence shell, it requires four more electrons to complete the octet. This gives carbon a combining capacity, or valency, of four, and the property is called tetravalency. Losing or gaining four electrons is highly unlikely for an atom of carbon's small size because both processes would require far too much energy; therefore, carbon completes its octet by sharing its four valence electrons with other atoms. The bond formed by the mutual sharing of electron pairs between two combining atoms is known as a covalent bond. A single carbon atom can form four covalent bonds, and these bonds may be with four different atoms or with other carbon atoms.

The second remarkable property of carbon is catenation, which is the ability of carbon atoms to link with one another to form long straight chains, branched chains, and closed rings. This self-bonding capacity of carbon is much stronger and more varied than that of any other element. In a carbon chain, each carbon atom is linked to one, two, or three other carbon atoms and also to other atoms such as hydrogen. The chains may be straight like those in the molecules of methane and ethane when they are extended into larger alkanes such as propane, branched like those found in higher alkanes, or arranged in rings as in the benzene molecule. Because of tetravalency, each carbon atom in a chain can also hold other atoms or groups; because of catenation, the chains can grow long and take many shapes. These two properties together explain why carbon forms the basis of an enormous number of compounds, collectively known as organic compounds. Carbon can also form multiple covalent bonds, such as the double bond it forms with oxygen in carbon dioxide and the double bonds that appear between adjacent carbon atoms in benzene. All these bonding abilities make carbon the central element in the chemistry of living things, fuels, plastics, medicines, and countless other substances used in daily life in homes, schools, and laboratories across India.
eli5: Imagine an atom of carbon as a tiny friend with four open hands. It can hold onto four other friends at the same time by sharing. Carbon can hold hands with other carbon friends too, making long lines, branches, and circles. That is why carbon can build so many different things, from the gas that cooks our food to the rings that make special smells.

misconceptions.belief: Some students think that carbon has an unstable electronic configuration and therefore forms ionic compounds. This is reflected in the exam guidance where candidates chose "It has unstable electronic configuration" as an incorrect reason for carbon's behaviour. The correction is that carbon's electronic configuration 2,4 is not unstable; it is tetravalent, meaning it has valency 4 and forms four covalent bonds by sharing electrons, not by losing or gaining them.

Some students cannot distinguish between covalent and ionic compounds and confuse carbon tetrachloride with ionic compounds like sodium chloride. The examiner notes state that "Some candidates chose the incorrect option NaCl as they had no idea that CCl4 is a covalent compound." The correction is that CCl4 is a covalent compound because carbon and chlorine share electrons to complete their octets, whereas sodium chloride is ionic because sodium transfers an electron to chlorine.

Some students confuse the bonding of carbon with other types of bonding and forget that catenation is the special reason for the large number of organic compounds. The examiners have observed candidates being confused between different bonding concepts, which suggests a weak grasp of fundamentals. The correction is that covalent bonds in carbon compounds are formed by the sharing of electrons, and the large number of carbon compounds arises from both tetravalency and catenation together, not from tetravalency alone.

diagnosticQuestions.question: Define tetravalency and catenation. Write the electronic configuration of carbon and explain how these three facts are related to one another.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: Tetravalency is the property of an element, in this case carbon, by which it has a valency of four. Carbon has the atomic number 6, so its electronic configuration is 2,4. This means it has two electrons in the first shell and four electrons in the outermost or valence shell. To become stable by completing the octet in the outermost shell, carbon needs four more electrons. Because four is a large number for a small atom, carbon does not lose or gain four electrons; instead it shares its four valence electrons with other atoms. This sharing of electron pairs is called covalent bonding, and it is the reason a single carbon atom can form four covalent bonds. Catenation is the ability of carbon atoms to bond with one another and form long chains, branched chains, and rings. The combination of tetravalency and catenation makes carbon the basis of a vast number of organic compounds. If carbon were only tetravalent but could not bond to itself, the number of carbon compounds would be very small. If it could only bond to itself but did not have valency 4, it could not hold the many different side atoms that give organic chemistry its variety.

diagnosticQuestions.question: Why does carbon form covalent bonds rather than ionic bonds? Explain with reference to its electronic configuration.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: Carbon forms covalent bonds rather than ionic bonds because of its small size and its electronic configuration of 2,4. In an ionic bond, one atom transfers one or more electrons to another atom, and the resulting oppositely charged ions attract each other. For carbon to form an ionic compound, it would have to either lose four electrons to become C^4^+ or gain four electrons to become C^4^-. A small atom like carbon cannot hold such a high positive charge, because the remaining electrons would be pulled strongly by the nucleus, and a C^4^- ion would be equally unstable because the added electrons would be too close together and would repel one another. Instead, carbon uses the easier and more stable method of sharing electrons. It shares one pair of electrons with each of four other atoms, forming four covalent bonds. This way, carbon effectively has eight electrons in its outer shell, satisfying the octet rule, without creating highly charged ions. That is why substances such as methane, ethane, and carbon tetrachloride are covalent compounds.

diagnosticQuestions.question: "Carbon forms a large number of compounds only because it has four electrons in its outermost shell." Evaluate this statement.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: This statement is partly correct but not fully true, and a good student should explain both the correct part and the missing part. It is true that carbon has four electrons in its outermost shell, giving it a valency of 4 or tetravalency. This means one carbon atom can form four covalent bonds with other atoms, which is essential for building molecules. However, the statement is incomplete because it does not account for catenation, which is the ability of carbon atoms to bond with one another to form long chains, branched chains, and rings. Many other elements also have a valency greater than one, but none of them can link with themselves in the many different ways that carbon can. If carbon only had tetravalency, each carbon atom could bond to four other atoms, but the atoms would have to be different elements; there would be no long carbon chains, no branches, and no rings. It is the combination of tetravalency and catenation that makes carbon the basis of the vast number of organic compounds. Therefore, the statement should be accepted as a partial explanation but rejected if it is meant to be a complete explanation. The better statement is: "Carbon forms a large number of compounds because it is tetravalent and shows catenation."

diagnosticQuestions.question: Describe how carbon forms bonds in methane and in ethane. In each case, state the number of covalent bonds around a carbon atom and whether the carbon-carbon or carbon-hydrogen bonds are single or double.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: In methane, the formula is CH4. The carbon atom is in the centre and is bonded to four hydrogen atoms. Each bond is formed by the sharing of one pair of electrons between the carbon atom and a hydrogen atom. Because only one pair of electrons is shared in each bond, all four carbon-hydrogen bonds are single covalent bonds. The carbon atom has four single covalent bonds, which satisfies its valency of 4. In ethane, the formula is C2H6. The two carbon atoms are bonded to each other by one single covalent bond formed by the sharing of one pair of electrons. Each carbon atom is also bonded to three hydrogen atoms by single covalent bonds. Therefore, each carbon atom has four single covalent bonds in total: one to the other carbon atom and three to hydrogen atoms. In neither methane nor ethane is there a double bond; double bonds in carbon compounds are seen in substances such as ethene or carbon dioxide, where two pairs of electrons are shared between two bonded atoms. The single covalent bonds in methane and ethane show how carbon uses its tetravalency to build simple molecules.

diagnosticQuestions.question: Imagine you have to design a new model to teach Class 5 students why carbon forms so many compounds. Describe at least three features of your model, including how you would explain tetravalency, catenation, and the difference between a carbon chain and a carbon ring.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: My model would be a hands-on activity using everyday materials. The first feature is a set of four Velcro strips attached to a central ball representing the carbon atom; these strips represent the four valence electrons and show that carbon can hold four other balls. This explains tetravalency because each Velcro strip can attach to one other ball, and the carbon ball can never hold more than four. The second feature is a string of paper clips linked together to show catenation. Each paper clip is a carbon atom and the links between clips are covalent bonds. I can make a straight chain to show a carbon chain like that in ethane or propane, and I can bend the chain into a circle to show a carbon ring like benzene. The third feature is a branched structure made by connecting one paper-clip chain to the side of another, so students can see that carbon chains need not be straight. To explain the difference between a chain and a ring, I would say that a chain has two ends, like a train, while a ring has no ends, like a necklace of beads. The model would close with the message that because carbon can make four bonds and can also bond to itself, it can build millions of different molecules, which is why carbon is the element of life and the basis of organic chemistry.

masteryCriteria: Can explain that carbon forms covalent bonds by sharing electrons (tetravalent: 4 bonds); can define catenation (carbon chains with itself); can distinguish single (C-C), double (C=C), and triple (C===C) bonds; can give one example of each (ethane, ethene, ethyne).

title: Physical and chemical changes - advanced
subject: chem
definition:
A physical change is a change in which the form, size, shape or state of a substance alters, but no new substance is produced. The particles making up the matter remain the same; only their arrangement, spacing or motion changes. For example, when ice is heated it becomes water, and with more heating it becomes steam. In every case the tiny water particles are still the same, only their freedom of movement and separation have increased. Other familiar physical changes include expansion, in which a solid, liquid or gas takes up more space on heating because its particles vibrate or move faster and push further apart; evaporation, in which a liquid changes into a vapour at the surface; condensation, the reverse process in which a gas turns into a liquid on cooling; freezing, in which a liquid becomes a solid; and sublimation, in which a solid turns directly into a gas without passing through the liquid state. Many physical changes are reversible, which means the original substance can be obtained back again by reversing the condition, usually by cooling or by removing heat. Some physical changes, such as tearing paper or breaking a glass tumbler, may be irreversible because the pieces cannot easily be put back together, even though no new chemical substance has been formed.

A chemical change, on the other hand, is a change in which one or more new substances are formed. The original particles are rearranged or split apart and combine differently, giving products with new properties. Signs of a chemical change include a change in colour, the production of a gas with bubbling or effervescence, the formation of a precipitate, the release or absorption of heat or light, and the appearance of a new smell. Burning is a common chemical change in which a substance reacts with oxygen to give new products such as carbon dioxide and water. When a candle burns, two things happen at the same time. The heat of the flame melts the solid wax near the wick; this melting is a physical change because the liquid wax can be cooled and will become solid wax again. At the same time, the hot wax vapour and the wick react with oxygen in the air; this burning is a chemical change because new substances, mainly carbon dioxide, water vapour and some carbon particles, are formed. This is why the burning of a candle is one of the most important examples in this chapter: it shows that heating can cause a physical change and a chemical change together. The vocabulary of this topic, physical change, chemical change, expansion, change of state, evaporation, condensation, freezing, sublimation, burning, heating, candle, reversible and irreversible, must be used accurately in board answers because each term carries a precise scientific meaning that examiners look for.
eli5: When you heat something, it can get bigger or change from solid to liquid or gas, but it is still the same stuff. That is a physical change. If it turns into something new that you cannot change back easily, like ash or smoke, that is a chemical change. A candle does both: the wax melts from the heat, but the wax also burns to make new things.

misconceptions.belief: "A change of state, like ice turning into steam, is a chemical change because the appearance is completely different." board examiner observations show that pupils often give vague or incomplete answers and fail to name the precise process. For example, exam guidance in Common board exam error pattern note that many candidates wrote 'water' instead of the correct specific term or role, and the remedy given was to review topic fundamentals. In the same way, a student may say that water changes into steam but forget that the water particles are still the same. The correction is that a change of state is a physical change; the substance remains H2O throughout and the change can be reversed by cooling or compressing the vapour.

"Burning a candle is only a chemical change because it gives out heat and light." Common board exam error pattern comments for 2024 and 2025 repeatedly point out that candidates confuse categories and leave out key terms or conditions; for instance, some omitted the term 'd-d transition' or confused paired and unpaired electrons, and others were unclear about reactants and products. The same pattern appears here when students see a flame and forget the melted wax. The correction is that the candle shows both physical and chemical changes. The melting of wax is physical, while the reaction of wax vapour with oxygen to form carbon dioxide and water is chemical.

"Sublimation is a chemical change because the solid disappears and a new gas is formed." Common board exam error pattern comments note that many candidates could not write correct balanced equations and were confused about the identity of reactants and products. This carries over to sublimation, where students think the solid has been destroyed. The correction is that in sublimation the solid simply becomes a gas directly; the particles remain the same substance, and the change can be reversed by cooling the gas back to a solid. No new chemical substance is formed.

diagnosticQuestions.question: Distinguish between a physical change and a chemical change. Give one example of each and list two signs that help you decide a chemical change has taken place.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: A physical change is a change in the size, shape or state of a substance in which no new substance is formed and the particles remain the same. For example, when ice is heated it becomes water, and the water can be frozen back to ice; this is a reversible change of state. A chemical change is a change in which one or more new substances are formed with different properties from the starting substance. For example, when a piece of paper burns in air it turns into ash and gases such as carbon dioxide, and the ash cannot be changed back into paper by simple cooling or pressing. The signs that help us recognise a chemical change include a change in colour, the evolution of a gas with bubbles or a smell, the formation of a solid precipitate, the production of heat or light, and the appearance of a new odour. A physical change may show a change in appearance, but it does not produce these permanent signs because the substance itself has not been chemically altered.

diagnosticQuestions.question: Ice is kept in a pan and heated until it turns into steam. Explain, step by step, whether the changes from ice to water and from water to steam are physical or chemical, and justify your answer using the idea of particles.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: When ice is placed in a pan and heated, the first change is the conversion of solid ice into liquid water. This is called melting or fusion, and it is a physical change because the water particles themselves are still the same H2O units; they only gain energy and begin to move more freely around each other. The shape and hardness of the ice have gone, but the substance has not become something new. The change can be reversed by removing heat and allowing the water to freeze again. Next, when the water is heated more, it turns into steam. This is evaporation, and it is also a physical change. The water particles now have enough energy to escape into the air as a gas, but each particle is still H2O. If the steam is cooled, for example by touching a cold lid, it condenses back to liquid water. Because no new substance has been formed at any stage, both melting and evaporation are physical changes. Only if the water were broken down into hydrogen and oxygen by very strong heating or by passing an electric current would a chemical change occur.

diagnosticQuestions.question: A student says, "Sublimation of camphor is a chemical change because the solid camphor disappears and a new gas with a strong smell is formed." Evaluate this statement, giving a balanced argument that considers both sides before reaching a conclusion.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: At first sight, the student's statement sounds reasonable because the camphor does seem to disappear and a strong smelling gas is noticed in the air. The substance that was once a white solid is no longer visible in the same place, and the vapour that spreads has a different appearance and smell. These observations might lead someone to think that a new substance has been produced, especially since the change is so obvious. However, a closer scientific look shows that the student is wrong. In sublimation, the solid camphor changes directly into camphor vapour, which is still camphor. The particles that make up the solid have only spread far apart; they have not broken apart and rearranged into different kinds of particles. This can be shown by allowing the vapour to cool on a cold surface; it deposits again as solid white camphor, proving that the original substance has been recovered. A chemical change would require a new substance with different properties, and that would not be reversible by a simple change in temperature. The smell is simply the camphour vapour reaching our nose, not a new chemical product. Therefore, the correct conclusion is that sublimation of camphor is a physical change, because it is a change of state that is reversible and no new substance is formed.

diagnosticQuestions.question: A friend argues that because wax melts and vanishes when a candle burns, the whole process is a physical change. Describe a simple investigation you could carry out to prove that a candle involves both a physical and a chemical change.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: To show that a candle involves both a physical and a chemical change, I would carry out two simple observations. First, I would hold a small piece of candle wax a short distance above a lighted candle so that it warms but does not burn. The wax would melt into a colourless liquid. I would then remove the heat and allow the liquid wax to cool. It would become solid wax again, with the same smell and appearance as before. This shows that melting is a physical, reversible change. Next, I would allow the candle to burn normally and hold a dry, cold glass plate or a metal spoon a few centimetres above the flame. After a few seconds, the inside surface of the plate would become covered with a black substance, which is carbon, and with tiny droplets of water. I would also show that the gas given out turns lime water milky, proving the presence of carbon dioxide. These products, carbon, water and carbon dioxide, are new substances with new properties, so the burning is a chemical change. Thus the candle shows both changes: melting of wax is physical, while burning is chemical.

diagnosticQuestions.question: Design a simple experiment that you could do at home to show that expansion on heating and evaporation are both physical changes. Your answer should list the materials, the steps, the expected observations and the reason for your conclusion.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: Materials needed are a clean glass bottle with a narrow neck, a one-holed rubber stopper that fits the bottle, a transparent drinking straw or a narrow glass tube, a small amount of coloured water, a large bowl of warm water and a cool, dry plate. Insert the straw through the stopper and fit the stopper tightly into the bottle neck after pouring in enough coloured water so that the liquid rises part way up the straw. Mark the level of the coloured water on the straw with a thin marker. Place the bottle in the bowl of warm water and watch the level. After a few minutes the coloured water will rise in the straw because the water expands on heating. Then remove the bottle and place it in a cool place. The liquid level will fall back to the original mark, showing that the change is reversible. For evaporation, take a small saucer of salt solution and leave it on a sunny windowsill. After some time, the water will evaporate and the salt will be left behind as a white solid. To show condensation, place a cool plate above the saucer so that the water vapour condenses on it and the drops can be collected. The water obtained by condensation is still water, and the salt can be dissolved again in fresh water. Since both the expansion of water and the evaporation of salt water can be reversed without forming a new substance, they are physical changes.

masteryCriteria: Can distinguish physical changes (reversible, no new substance: melting, dissolving) from chemical changes (irreversible, new substance: burning, rusting); can classify ten changes correctly; can explain energy changes in chemical reactions (exothermic releases heat, endothermic absorbs heat).
